title: Bombardier Beetle Optimizer (BBO) for Optimizing Engineering Design Problems
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive comparative study of various metaheuristic optimization algorithms with the intention of emphasizing the most adequate method for optimizing well-established design problems of engineering. The algorithms chosen for this study include “Bombardier Beetle Optimizer (BBO)”, “Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)”, and “Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO)”. The experimental results of this paper are extracted in two phases. In the first phase, these algorithms are utilized to optimize the “Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) 2017” test bed suite. While in the second phase, they are applied to solve the well-known problems of engineering design, such as Speed Reducer Design, Pressure Vessel Design, Cantilever Beam Design, and Robot Gripper optimization problems. Moreover, two techniques for evaluating the proposed algorithms are selected in this paper, which are quantitative and qualitative analyses. For the former one, a set of key performance indicators are used to measure solution quality, which are mean, best fitness, and standard deviation. While for the later one, the convergence curves are drawn to estimate the efficiency of algorithms over iterations. This helps for a robust estimation of each algorithm's ability to poise exploration and exploitation in the domain of any problem. These case studies provide more evidence of the algorithms' versatility and applicability in managing challenging, multifaceted, and limited optimization jobs. The outcomes show that BBO has the merit in optimizing these problems.

title: Photonic convolution neural networks for machine learning via energy-free Fourier-optics
abstract: Convolutional operations are computationally intensive in artificial intelligence (AI) services, and their overhead in electronic hardware limits machine learning scaling. Here, we introduce a photonic joint transform correlator (pJTC) using a near-energy-free on-chip Fourier transformation to accelerate convolution operations. The pJTC reduces computational complexity for both convolution and cross-correlation from O(N^4) to O(N^2) , where N2 is the input data size. Demonstrating functional Fourier transforms and convolution, this pJTC achieves 98.0% accuracy on an exemplary Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology inference task. Furthermore, a wavelength-multiplexed pJTC architecture shows potential for high throughput and energy efficiency, reaching 305 TOPS/W and 40.2 TOPS/mm^2, based on currently available foundry processes. An efficient, compact, and low-latency convolution accelerator promises to advance next-generation AI capabilities across edge demands, high-performance computing, and cloud services.

The pJTC reduces computational complexity for both convolution and cross-correlation from O(N^4) to O(N^2) , where N2 is the input data size. Demonstrating functional Fourier transforms and convolution, this pJTC achieves 98.0% accuracy on an exemplary Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology inference task. Furthermore, a wavelength-multiplexed pJTC architecture shows potential for high throughput and energy efficiency, reaching 305 TOPS/W and 40.2 TOPS/mm^2, based on currently available foundry processes. An efficient, compact, and low-latency convolution accelerator promises to advance next-generation AI capabilities across edge demands, high-performance computing, and cloud services.

title: Hamiltonian-Dependent Compressibility and Physical Preservation in Approximate Quantum Compilation using Tensor Networks
abstract: Approximate quantum compilation (AQC) using tensor networks provides a promising route to reducing the circuit resources required for quantum simulation. However, the factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and the extent to which compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions using AQCtensor for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a Néel state. By varying the exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field, we find that compression performance changes systematically with the anisotropic coupling configuration and field orientation. These variations are strongly associated with a nested-commutator measure related to second-order Trotter error, with corresponding directional trends also reflected in the target-state MPS bond dimension. For an 80-qubit quantum-hardware evaluation, AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing the total circuit depth by 45.9% and the two-qubit gate count by 47.6%. The compressed circuit exhibits comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements, while process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography provide complementary characterization beyond these observables. Together, these results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity and demonstrate substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems for Knowledge-Grounded Material Substitution
abstract: AI-assisted scientific discovery increasingly seeks to move beyond generating plausible ideas toward reproducible, constraint-aware workflows that can support practical engineering decisions. We present MARS, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning System for knowledge-grounded material substitution under scientific and manufacturing constraints. We apply MARS to replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a demanding materials-design problem in which substitutes must satisfy functional performance, environmental, experimental, and processing requirements. MARS decomposes substitution into a closed-loop workflow comprising requirement analysis, grounded candidate generation, and manufacturability assessment with process design. The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, a database of lab-available materials, persistent memory of intermediate results, and rejection-aware iterative feedback. In a PFAS-substitution case study, MARS generates structured material requirements, identifies an evidence-grounded substitute candidate, and develops a lab-scale manufacturing route. In a multi-seed ablation evaluation, MARS achieves the highest overall performance across all three subsystems, with gains that persist when the backbone model is held fixed. These results suggest that hierarchical decomposition, knowledge grounding, and manufacturability-aware refinement improve material-substitution reasoning beyond model capability alone.

title: GPU-Based Parallel BP Decoding for Quantum LDPC Memory
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) decoding requires reliable corrections and low latency over long syndrome histories. We extend BP-SF, an oscillation-guided belief-propagation (BP) decoder with independent syndrome-flip trials, by introducing windowed and streaming operations. Our CUDA implementation combines disordered-memory retries, sliding windows, correlation-aware graphs, and layered scheduling. Circuit-level simulations test fixed-basis memory and complete logical Pauli-frame recovery. On the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code at physical error rate p = 0.002, parallel BP-SF reduces 99.9th-percentile call latency by a factor of 13.15 relative to an eight-chain Relay-BP GPU baseline on 100,000 matched samples for which every tested method's initial BP stage fails within 80 iterations. Windowed BP-SF maintains a flat logical error rate and nearly constant per-round compute time through 512 rounds, reaching a 17.1-fold speedup over monolithic decoding. In 512-round full-frame streaming decoding with 2.97-ms syndrome arrivals, layered BP-SF on a transformed joint graph with 20 retries reduces 99.9th-percentile correction-release age from 166.29 to 36.25 ms relative to the joint graph with flooding updates and 100 retries. These results connect parallel BP post-processing to lower decoding costs and earlier correction release in streaming quantum memory.

title: SLICE: Sequential Likelihood-Free Inference via Conformal E-Values
abstract: Many scientific models can be simulated but have intractable likelihoods, making frequentist uncertainty quantification difficult. We construct exact anytime-valid confidence sequences for the parameters of such models. At each observation, fresh simulations from each candidate null conformalize a positive predictable score into a conditional e-value; their product is a test martingale, which we invert over the parameter. Validity holds for any such score, whatever its accuracy. We show that the oracle likelihood-ratio score maximizes expected log growth, which motivates approximating it with an amortized neural ratio estimator. On synthetic benchmarks, an audit of model routing in an LLM API, and microlensing data, the resulting confidence sequences stay valid under continuous monitoring, where fixed-sample methods do not, and neural scores remain competitive with exact likelihood ratios and application-specific scores.

title: GuidedNav: Shaping Vision-Language Navigation Representations through Pre-action Attention and Spatial Guidance
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to track progress through an extended instruction, identify landmarks relevant to its current objective, and understand the surrounding spatial structure to act. End-to-end navigation policies typically rely on action supervision to implicitly learn these capabilities. Without explicit guidance on the evidence underlying each decision, however, policies can overfit to correlations predictive of training actions rather than learn the task-relevant grounding and geometry needed for generalization. Our insight is to guide the representations that connect instructions to actions: identifying what remains to be done determines which visual evidence matters, while understanding the geometry around that evidence informs how to move. We introduce GuidedNav, a unified framework that explicitly shapes these representations through training-time guidance. Subtask and landmark guidance steer native pre-action attention toward the active instruction segment and relevant visual regions, grounding action prediction in the current objective. Spatial guidance aligns the policy's internal representations with geometric features that capture long-horizon context and local spatial structure. Together, these objectives strengthen navigation capabilities while avoiding the inference overhead of intermediate textual reasoning and online geometric encoding. We also introduce Guided-R2R and Guided-RxR, two annotation-enriched navigation datasets that support more interpretable VLN research. GuidedNav establishes state-of-the-art performance among the compared monocular RGB policies, improving success rates by 8.1% and 13.1% relative to the strongest prior results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen, respectively, while achieving faster inference. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and real-world transferability of our approach.

title: Temporal-Access Resource Theory for Continuous Process Tensors
abstract: The uncontrolled endpoint channel can conceal how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control. We formulate a fixed-task resource theory of continuous process tensors with physical access interfaces, entrance-erasing free objects, and budgeted free conversions. Complete-record total-variation error measures performance; the calibrated capability is monotone under conversions that preserve a common free baseline. For unknown-state transmission the baseline is exactly $1-d^{-2}$. Two qubit processes with the same endpoint channel have optimal errors $0$ and $p=\sin^2(2gh)$ at the same finite pulse budget in an ideal-transparent system-only window architecture, forcing any endpoint-only predictor to err by at least $p/2$ on one of them. An exactly solvable family shows how the allocation of a fixed interaction phase around a control window sets the attainable error, and a nontrivial perfect echo requires and attains total control action $π$ in that architecture. The separation extends directly to every qubit unitary target at a budget that includes its boundary gate, while unitary tasks in any dimension have baseline $1-d^{-2}$ whenever a budget-feasible free realization gives the depolarizing output. Complete-record implementation bounds quantify coherent and dissipative control imperfections. Continuous-process randomized compilation supplies physical instrument pullbacks; compatible completion conditions extend their action, and certified dynamical bounds yield achievable task-error and capability guarantees. The resulting theory identifies temporal structure and control investment that endpoint characterization alone cannot resolve.

title: O'ZBEKCHA-RUSCHA PARALLEL KORPUSLARI ASOSIDA ALIGNER TIZIMINI YARATISHDA NLP TEXNOLOGIYALARI
abstract: Mazkur maqolada o‘zbek va rus tillari o‘rtasidagi parallel korpuslar asosida avtomatik aligner tizimini ishlab chiqish masalasi yoritiladi. Parallel korpuslar mashina tarjimasi, lingvistik tahlil va til modellarini o‘qitishda muhim resurs bo‘lib, o‘zbek tilining resurs jihatdan kam ta’minlanganligi ushbu yo‘nalishda maxsus yondashuvlarni talab etadi. Tadqiqotda parallel matnlarni yig‘ish, preprocessing, tokenizatsiya, gaplarga ajratish va normalizatsiya bosqichlari amalga oshirilgan. Gaplar darajasidagi moslashtirish uchun uzunlikka asoslangan Gale–Church algoritmi, lexical-based yondashuv va statistik modellar elementlarini birlashtirgan gibrid model taklif etilgan. Tajriba natijalari gibrid yondashuvning boshqa alohida metodlarga nisbatan yuqori samaradorlik ko‘rsatganini ko‘rsatadi.

title: AICybOps: A Framework for Operationalizing Machine-Learning Models in Cybersecurity
abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used in cybersecurity, for example, for anomaly and intrusion detection in microservice and Internet of Things environments. Guidance on securing the machine learning operations (MLOps) lifecycle, termed MLSecOps or SecMLOps, recommends continuous monitoring, a versioned model registry, and lifecycle integration of training, evaluation, and serving. This layer is typically built per deployment, as model-specific code rather than a shared framework. We present AICybOps, a framework that systematizes these practices so the operational features and security properties a deployed model needs are provided by design. It wraps trained models behind a uniform lifecycle interface, exposes a monitor control application programming interface (API) for long-running prediction loops, re-loads models by registered name and version across hosts, and runs durable asynchronous training and evaluation, so a developer implements only the model and inherits the rest. These four design features constitute the framework’s current version; an inheritance-and-expansion criterion governs its contents and keeps it open to further security operations. Because the framework addresses a deployed model by registered version, tracks its runs automatically, and holds the registry behind the service boundary, it yields five security properties: lineage, reproducible replay, an audit trail, private provenance, and integrity of model identity.

title: DEEP LEARNING BASED CYBERBULLYING DETECTION ON SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS
abstract: Cyberbullying has become a major problem in social media, which poses severe psychological and emotional dangers to the users, especially adolescents and young adults.The explosive development of online communication has resulted in a rise in abusive and harmful content, which makes manual monitoring inefficient and impractical.The current systems of cyberbullying detection, which are mainly founded on the traditional machine learning techniques, are highly reliant on the detecting systems based on the analysis of keywords and lack the capacity to detect the contextual meaning, sarcasm, and linguistic variations, which contributes to the decreased accuracy and reliability.Recent works emphasize that deep learning methods are more successful than traditional ones because they are capable of capturing semantic and contextual relationships in textual data.The proposed research involves a deep learning-based system to detect cyberbullying based on a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) model.The system uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods that include text cleaning, text tokenization, removal of stop-words, and text normalization to preprocess text in social media.The word embeddings are used to convert the textual data to meaningful numerical representations so that the model can learn the semantic relationships between words.The BiLSTM architecture handles textual data both forward and backward, enabling it to effectively deal with contextual information and sequential dependencies.The proposed model is a multiclassification to discover the various categories of cyberbullying, in this case, agebased, gender-based, religious, and ethnic abuse.Experimental data has shown that the BiLSTM model can achieve the highest accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score than the traditional machine learning models.The system is scalable and can be deployed in real-time, which can help create safer online spaces as it can help detect and prevent cyberbullying content on the internet effectively.

title: Physics-informed deep learning with optical neural networks for information transmission through scattering media
abstract: We propose novel approachs to information transmission in scattering media such as multimode fibers (MMF). By utilizing the physical basis of the model, training with pure eigenmode data enables precise mode decomposition, which is of great importance in high-rate secure multimode fiber communication. In this work, we present physics-based deep learning methods for the mode demultiplexing (MD) of MMF. The "Physics-in-Loss" method utilizes the physical premise that an MMF represents the linear superposition of its eigenmodes. This eliminates the need for large datasets and lengthy training sessions. MD of over 5,000 modes is achieved. However, mainly we focus on "Physics-in-Network" which is based on optical diffractive neural networks. It operates with minimal energy consumption and very low latency. For real-time mode demultiplexing, training with only eigenmode distributions is sufficient to achieve precise results. We will highlight the unique advantages, trade-offs and applications to information transmission via scattering media.

title: An Empirical Case Study of Prompt Engineering Strategies for Bypassing Multi-Layer Agent Security Defenses
abstract: The OpenClaw Security Attack and Defense Challenge evaluates AI agent robustness through a three-stage defense pipeline: skill file scanning (Stage 1), instruction safety evaluation (Stage 2), and attack trajectory scoring (Stage 3). This paper presents an empirical case study of prompt engineering strategies against these layers across 19 attack targets in Enterprise OA, E-commerce, and Smart Home scenarios. I document both successful and failed strategies, with an emphasis on the observed trade-off between instruction safety (Stage 2) and attack execution accuracy (Stage 3). The final online score is 0.2630, with 5 of 19 tasks achieving full bypass. The results suggest that multi-layer defenses, reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints, substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.

title: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Fully Discrete Conditional Diffusion Models
abstract: We establish finite-sample guarantees for conditional diffusion models learned from data and implemented with finitely many denoising steps. Our approach aligns the score-training objective with the sampling grid, allowing statistical estimation and numerical discretization errors to be analyzed together. Under a smooth conditional density model, we derive high-probability bounds on the generated distribution's error and quantify the required number of score evaluations. For every smoothness index $β>0$, a suitable grid yields averaged conditional Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence $\widetilde O_p(n^{-2β/(d_x+d_y+2β)})$ relative to the original target with or without early stopping. Both the full and early-stopped samplers attain average target total-variation (TV) error $\widetilde O_p(n^{-β/(d_x+d_y+2β)})$. Here $n$ is the sample size, $d_x,d_y$ are the data and conditioning dimensions, and errors are averaged over the conditioning variable. The total-variation bound matches the rate established in existing conditional distribution-estimation theory, up to logarithmic factors.

title: Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport
abstract: We discuss three simple connections between generative diffusion and optimal transport. First, the joint law of the data and of their Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noising is, at every time, the solution of an entropic optimal-transport problem, at a temperature set by the noise level. Backward diffusion can consequently be read as an annealing which gradually decreases the entropic regularization. Second, we study the speciation transition--how the modes of the data distribution emerge during generation--and compare how it happens in diffusion and flow matching with respect to optimal transport. Using Gaussian mixtures as high-dimensional example, we show that the dynamical instability through which diffusion and flow matching separate the modes becomes, for optimal transport, an exponentially thin boundary layer at the beginning of generation, which is rounded by entropic regularization. Third, considering a generic forward dynamics with a general confining potential, we show that the backward process driven by the score also satisfies a drift-based variational principle whose minimal cost is the entropy difference between initial and final distributions.

title: ATHLETE: Learning Reactive Humanoid Tennis via Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching
abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher--student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of $90.00\%$ and $86.67\%$, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.

title: Win-Win Fusion: Multi-Modal Image Fusion with Visual-Semantic Collaboration
abstract: Existing multi-modal image fusion (MMIF) methods generally face an optimization gap between the visual and semantic domains, limiting the enhancement of perception capabilities. To overcome this long-standing barrier, this work proposes W2F, a new visual-semantic mutual reinforcing paradigm for MMIF. First, we reinforce the foundation for visual-semantic collaboration by amplifying feature complementarity through two targeted designs. Specifically, the segmentation-guided fusion loss introduces object-aware structural guidance into visual fusion, while the embedded information restoration prior strengthens the ability of visual fusion to provide reliable perceptual evidence for the semantic branch under degraded conditions. Then, we introduce a strong multi-modal information interaction mechanism composed of interactive gated mixed attention (IGM-Att) and progressive coupling attention (PC-Att). These modules ensure comprehensive scene representation from both local and global perspectives, providing informational support for visual-semantic collaboration. Finally, we construct a collaborative mechanism to couple visual fusion and semantic fusion. It employs a feature search module to extract complementary key features from both tasks, enriching the representational potential of visual and semantic information. Meanwhile, a gradient correction strategy ensures collaboration from the optimization perspective, enhancing performance for both visual and semantic fusion through consistency learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that W2F surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both visual appeal and decision accuracy. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaoZhang1018/W2F.

title: A Review on Explainable AI (XAI)
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive and detailed review on the topic of Explainable AI (XAI). This paper covers what XAI is, how it operates, notable use cases of it and current problems hindering it. Crucial XAI techniques such as LIME, SHAP and Open the Black Box are also discussed thoroughly in this paper. Finally, this paper concludes by stating that XAI will play an indispensable role in the field of artificial intelligence and the future as AI becomes more prominent in our modern society. Thus, the need for transparent and interpretable AI systems will be provided by XAI.

title: The pure-state ECQC conjecture: counterexamples and a prime-dimensional classification
abstract: Complete written proof and exact checkers for the pure-state prime-dimensional ECQC question: it holds universally exactly at p=2; every odd prime has a full-Schmidt-rank pure-state counterexample; dimensions 3 and 5 attain the sharp pure-state ratios 3/2 and 5/2. The three-dimensional witness has a separate complete Lean proof, but the full prime-dimensional classification is not claimed Lean-complete. This record explicitly distinguishes prior mixed-state counterexamples and does not claim first priority. The fixed immutable GitHub Release is https://github.com/mxym/math/releases/tag/ecqc-pure-state-classification-v1. AI-assisted research and writing; no external funding. Existing licenses and third-party notices are retained.

title: Integer Codes Correcting Single Sparse-Byte Errors and Detecting Double Sparse-Byte Errors
abstract: Sparse-byte error-control codes were originally developed mainly for protecting wide-I/O semiconductor memories, whereas their application to communication systems has received considerably less attention. In communication receivers, sparse-byte errors may arise from self-synchronous descrambling as well as from various byte-oriented operations. In this paper, we propose a class of integer codes capable of correcting single sparse-byte errors and detecting double sparse-byte errors. The proposed codes are defined over integer rings and constructed with the help of a computer search. To assess their efficiency, the proposed codes are compared with linear codes having similar error-control capabilities. We also investigate the potential of the proposed codes for practical implementation on modern processors. For this purpose, we use an analytical model of an eight-core processor. The obtained results show that, at a processor clock frequency of 4.5 GHz, the considered 32-bit codes achieve a theoretical encoding throughput of 144 Gbps and a minimum theoretical decoding throughput of 57.88 Gbps. These results indicate that the proposed approach has potential to be applied as a software-based solution for error control in modern communication systems.

title: Context-Enhanced Multimodal Learning Framework for Effective Hateful Meme Detection
abstract: Hateful memes carry harm through the complex combination of image and text, requiring a detector to analyze both modalities jointly. This study investigates whether a short, text-aware semantic description of each meme, generated once by a small vision-language model, adds complementary information beyond direct image-text cross-attention. Qwen2-VL-2B generates a two-to-three sentence description for every meme based on its visual content and overlaid text. Frozen CLIP and RoBERTa encode the visual, textual, and semantic description streams, while a trainable fusion head integrates them via bidirectional cross-attention with a learned gating mechanism. We evaluate our framework on the Facebook Hateful Memes dataset (9,000 labeled memes) using group-aware five-fold cross-validation across 5 random seeds. Across the Facebook Hateful Memes benchmark, the Qwen2-VL-augmented architecture yields an average AUROC reaching 0.8180 alongside a 0.6575 F1-score, noticeably surpassing both uncaptioned baselines (0.7230 AUROC) and control setups using permuted descriptions (0.7995 AUROC) Furthermore, evaluation across additional datasets—MAMI (Misogyny) and HarMeme (Social/COVID Harm)—demonstrates strong out-of-domain generalization (0.7680 and 0.7980 AUROC, respectively). Description-removal ablations confirm that intermediate semantic interpretations bridge subtle visual-textual incongruities, while cross-attention gating selectively filters description noise.

title: When Pleasing the User Compromises Care: AI Sycophancy in Caregiver-Mediated Healthcare
abstract: Large language model (LLM) alignment often assumes that the user interacting with a model is also the primary beneficiary of its behavior. Yet in many consequential settings, one person directs the system while another bears the consequences. We study this problem in caregiver-mediated healthcare, where parents, pet owners, and caregivers make decisions for children, animals, and older adults. We introduce an evidence-grounded benchmark spanning veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care, and test whether AI advisors maintain appropriate care when users express clinically inferior preferences. Holding patient facts fixed, we vary stated care preferences and communication styles and evaluate both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-up. Across frontier and open-weight models, inferior preferences substantially increase switching from appropriate to inappropriate care beyond neutral conversational drift and increase agreement with the requested action, while communication style alone has a smaller effect. These failures accumulate across turns, including on cases models initially answer correctly, and often carry moderate or severe potential harm. In matched eldercare cases, the effect of an inferior preference is similar whether it is expressed by the patient or by a caregiver. Together with models' limited tendency to elicit patient preferences in caregiver conversations, this suggests that current models are highly sensitive to expressed user preferences but less sensitive to whose preferences are represented and who bears the consequences. Our results expose a broader limitation of user-centric alignment in settings with multiple stakeholders.

title: Inference-Time Steering Across Scaffolds and Epitopes for Sample-Efficient De Novo Nanobody Design
abstract: Generative molecular design typically relies on over-generation and post-hoc filtering. Inference-time steering methods like Feynman-Kac (FK) steering improve efficiency by biasing trajectories toward high-reward candidates, yet they optimize within a single fixed configuration. In de novo nanobody design, upfront commitment to conditioning choices like scaffold identity or target epitope creates a bottleneck. Since yield varies across these conditions, steering unpromising setups wastes compute. We recast generative condition selection as an inference-time resource-allocation problem. We propose two dynamic budget allocators: a joint Global Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations concurrently, and a decoupled approach adapting Batched Successive Elimination (BaSE). Empirically, these dynamic allocators increase the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly 5$\times$ without sacrificing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.

title: CUBE: Class-conditioned Unknown Boundary Evidence for Open-Set Insect Species Recognition
abstract: Open-set insect species recognition faces significant challenges when deployed in real-world biodiversity scenarios, particularly when encountering unknown species that are visually close to known training classes. Unlike generic out-of-distribution samples, fine-grained unknown insects are often not visually anomalous. They instead tend to appear near the decision boundary of specific known species, leading to unreliable closed-set predictions. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Class-conditioned Unknown Boundary Evidence (CUBE)}, a novel evidence-based framework that models unknownness around each known species rather than as a single global unknown class. Our key idea is to evaluate a test sample relative to the known species it most closely resembles, enabling local rejection for visually confusable unknown insects. CUBE learns class-conditioned boundary evidence from auxiliary species, preserves auxiliary species as shadow references during inference, and incorporates taxonomic candidate calibration to verify biological plausibility. When ecological metadata is available, we further introduce CUBE-E, which adds a lightweight location-consistency term without modifying the visual backbone. Experiments on the Open-Insect C-America benchmark show that CUBE achieves superior performance, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines with 95.8\%, 98.7\%, and 99.1\% AUROC on local, non-local, and non-moth unknown splits, respectively, while maintaining 94.9\% closed-set accuracy. With ecological metadata, CUBE-E further improves the results to 96.0\%, 99.7\%, and 99.5\% AUROC with 95.2\% closed-set accuracy.

title: Test-Time Memory Construction
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.

title: Replaying the Movie in Your Mind Decoding Dynamic Visual Perception and Recall from EEG
abstract: Decoding dynamic visual content from EEG has advanced rapidly for visual perception, yet it remains unclear which aspects of neural representations are preserved when people internally replay dynamic scenes. We introduce PAIR, an EEG benchmark collected from 20 participants using an interleaved, clip-wise paradigm that pairs naturalistic video viewing with immediate visual recall. This design enables a comparison between externally driven perception and internally generated recall for the same stimulus content within a fixed trial sequence. We benchmark multiple decoding models on hierarchical semantic classification at both fine-grained and coarse-grained levels, meta-feature decoding tasks covering motion, color, object number, face, and human presence, and a state-decoding task that discriminates perception from recall. Within-subject validation results show numerically similar performance for several model--task combinations, alongside higher perception accuracy in two coarse-grained comparisons after multiple-comparison correction. In contrast, perception and recall are highly separable at the state level under the present validation protocol. State accuracy remains high after alpha-band ablation, although this does not exclude ocular or other task-related contributions.

title: When AI Makes Work Cheap, What Becomes Valuable?
abstract: As AI lowers the cost of generating ideas, exploring alternatives, and carrying out work, what remains scarce, and who will capture the value? This one-page business brief explains why cheaper proposals can increase the importance of trustworthy evidence, accumulated experience, and judgment about which checks deserve investment. It introduces technical capital as reusable knowledge and systems that improve future work, including proven methods, reliable tools, and lessons preserved with the conditions that made them valid. An illustrative manufacturing example shows how inexpensive screening, selective physical trials, and retained results can support continuing improvement. The brief distinguishes an impressive demonstration, a useful capability, and a durable profitable business, and explains why ownership of the visible AI interface does not automatically determine value capture. It is a general-audience companion to Brad Pierce’s technical report, When Design Exploration Gets Cheap: Upstream Search, Downstream Truth, and the Migration of Scarcity in Chip Design (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23256253). Prepared with AI assistance.

title: The Self-Healing Tower: Error Detection and Repair Built on Neal's Net
abstract: Neal's Net, the sum-to-ten mirror structure of the Fibonacci 60-ring, gives a body of exact digit laws, proven and developed in the companion system paper. This paper engineers those laws into a working repair architecture and measures it. A single ring already corrects any one fault from its own budget. Run every law together, the mirror, the locked square, Cassini, the parity and third-turn grids, the box and the twin grid's rectangle with its quarter-reflections, and the ring becomes a 435-check lattice; and because every moment of the ring is a known constant, the cells its broken checks point at are solved outright from the ring's own totals, measured at 100.0% clean through 21 scattered faults out of sixty and 99.2% at 24, with silent errors 0.0% at every row. Carry data in frames and stack the frames into a fractal tower, levels that verify levels and checksums that are themselves protected data, and whole dead frames rebuild from the sums above them, twin-pair losses recover, and damage inside the checksums heals from the parent level, with delivery certified or flagged and never silently wrong. Measured on a 900-digit payload with the damage sprayed over every stored digit, the cells, the three root copies and the pillar keys alike, the tower is 100.0% clean through 40 flips and 60 erased cells, still 99.4% at 80 flips and 98.0% at 240 erased cells, rebuilds a whole killed frame, and delivers nothing wrong: silent deliveries are 0.00% at every point of every row, through 4,000 flips and 6,000 erasures, and 0.000% in a 3,000-trial deep check. Three integer moment totals, plain, weighted and quadratic, do the work: they detect, name the damaged cell directly, c = W/T confirmed by Q = T·c², and state the correction. The architecture is exercised end to end on a real task. A neural network trained under 174 seeded strikes inside the tower finishes with weights byte-identical to an untouched reference run, 0 of 7,440 bytes differ. The same totals guard arithmetic in flight: cells miscomputed inside a live integer matrix multiply are located and corrected exactly, 100.0% from one fault through 768 simultaneous faults on a 256 × 256 tile, with zero silent deliveries at every measured level, and with eight witness families through 4,096. The guard carries onto floating point without a hole. Checked on the fp32 accumulator with sign-randomized moment columns, a 303-million-parameter language model trained 12,000 steps on a TPU with every matrix product guarded, forward and both backward products, 111 operations, took 6,622 injected single-cell faults, caught 6,622, raised 0 false alarms in 24,000 guarded steps, and finished bit-identical to the guarded fault-free run, while the same faults unguarded left 99.9% of the weights different and the loss curve unchanged. Every number is measured, by enumeration where the claim is exact and by seeded trials elsewhere, and every boundary is stated, the overhead, the fault budgets, the rare worst-case escape rates, and the price of the float check at every width measured.

title: Transforming Archival Classification Schemes into a Knowledge Organization System (KOS) Based on SKOS and RiC-O: Implementation in Arteri-2
abstract: Government archival classification schemes are conventionally documented in static tabular formats, such as statutory regulatory decrees or closed relational database tables. This legacy representation severely restricts machine-readability, impedes inter-agency semantic interoperability, and reduces rich bureaucratic functional taxonomies to mere alphanumeric string prefixes for document numbering. This study adopts the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology integrated with Stanford's Ontology Development 101 engineering framework to transform public sector facilitative and substantive classification schemes into a formalized Knowledge Organization System (KOS).

title: Making Healthcare AI Explainable: A Structured Review of Methods and Clinical Practice
abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming modern medicine, providing powerful tools to assist clinicians. However, the most accurate models are opaque, and their limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption and raises regulatory concerns. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make these models’ decisions comprehensible. Despite its rapid growth and the many reviews already published, aspects such as the rigor of explanation evaluation, clinician involvement, and the use of large language models to generate explanations appear to have received limited attention. This article is a structured, relevance-prioritized review of XAI applied in healthcare, organized around six research questions covering the XAI techniques used, the data and clinical domains they are paired with, the models they explain, how evaluation is performed, the identified limitations, and the use of large language models. Unlike prior reviews that each address only part of this scope, we bring these dimensions together and quantify how rigorously explanations are evaluated and how often the underlying models are externally validated. We conducted a structured search across four literature sources: IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Google Scholar, and PubMed Central (PMC). We adapted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow by carrying a relevance-prioritized subset forward to full-text eligibility assessment, yielding 64 articles for synthesis. Within this corpus, our review revealed a predominantly image-based, post hoc XAI landscape dominated by a few established methods such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), mostly paired with convolutional, tree-based, and hybrid models on classification and risk-prediction tasks. Clinicians evaluated the explanations in only a minority of the included studies, and relatively few models were externally validated, with no evidence of large language models in our corpus. We conclude that stronger evaluation practices and closer collaboration with clinicians are needed to produce models that are clinically useful and safe to deploy.

title: SAFE-MedPath: Patient-Disjoint Breast Histopathology Classification with Calibration Transfer Analysis and Conformal Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Histopathology classifiers can be undermined by staining variability, patient-level data leakage, domain shift across tasks, and poorly calibrated probability outputs. We propose SAFE-MedPath, combining stain-oriented stochastic augmentation, a three-member ResNet-18 ensemble, post-hoc temperature scaling, and split-conformal prediction. BreaKHis is used for strictly patient-disjoint development, calibration, and testing; PatchCamelyon (PCam), whose endpoint (metastatic-tissue detection) differs from BreaKHis’s benign-versus-malignant task, is evaluated separately as an independent benchmark of architecture and training-recipe portability rather than same-task validation. Comparators are HOG+linear-SVM, HOG+RBF-SVM, and a single ResNet-18, all under an identical patient-disjoint protocol. On the BreaKHis test set, SAFE-MedPath achieved balanced accuracy 0.877 (95% CI 0.802–0.947), ROC-AUC 0.959, expected calibration error (ECE) 0.126, and split-conformal coverage 0.976 against a 0.90 target (mean prediction-set size 1.25). Ablation showed ensembling gave a small discrimination gain (+0.4 balanced-accuracy points) while stain augmentation and temperature scaling both hurt their target metric, indicating a validation-to-test calibration-transfer gap. On the independent PCam benchmark, the same architecture and recipe achieved balanced accuracy 0.821 and ROC-AUC 0.932. The full pipeline did not significantly improve discrimination over a single ResNet-18 (0.877 vs. 0.930; p=0.168 after Holm–Bonferroni correction), but converted that ensemble into a calibrated, uncertainty-aware output with 97.6% empirical coverage against a 90% target. The modest ensembling effect and calibration-transfer gap warrant further study before any clinical-use claim.

title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
abstract: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.

title: Compass in the Mirror: Quantum Backpropagation with the Hopf Ansatz
abstract: A variational quantum state may have many control angles, and its complete gradient contains one derivative for each. The task is to turn access to selected derivatives into a shared finite-shot record for the complete vector. The Hopf ansatz supplies the setting: it constructs any normalized pure state from nested two-way magnitude splits and, for complex states, leaf phases, with one directly programmed angle per split or phase. Earlier Hopf constructions prepare the state, recover coordinates from known amplitudes, and provide indexed derivative access. With a phase-calibrated controlled reflection, the inverse Hopf frame maps each normalized magnitude direction to a computational label, so every all-$X$ outcome contributes to every magnitude derivative. A separate signed leaf record supplies the complex phase block. A checkpoint variant reverses only the suffix below a selected depth and returns that layer's gradient block. For a complete chart with $M$ real-valued parameters, sufficient execution counts are $\mathcal{O}(\log\log M)$ for the global method and $\mathcal{O}(\log M\log\log M)$ for the complete checkpoint schedule at fixed additive coordinate accuracy and confidence. The global saving is record reuse, not a reduction of the $M$-entry output. Under the designated direct-angle schedules, the global method's assigned Hopf CNOT work and input/output-inclusive storage have at most logarithmic overhead relative to a matched scalar evaluation. The same Hopf geometry thus carries a state forward and the objective's complete coordinate response backward.

title: Returning to Development States: When Full Sandbox Snapshots Help Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents often make useful progress before they fail, but retry-from-scratch discards the machine state created along the way. This makes failure recovery an interesting search problem: if intermediate environment states preserve meaningful progress, restoring and branching from them could outperform repeatedly restarting from the initial state. We implement Go-Explore-style search over full Daytona snapshots and find that higher and more efficient solve rates depend mainly on progress that sits outside the repository, such as databases, services, and other runtime state. Our results suggest that full-snapshot search is most effective when long-horizon coding work spans multiple services whose state cannot be reconstructed from a single diff.

title: Why DiT Models Underperform as Representation Learners without Long Skip Connections
abstract: Diffusion feature, i.e., intermediate activations extracted from diffusion model backbones, has emerged as a promising approach for unifying generation and vision understanding (discrimination). Despite the advancement of diffusion backbones into Diffusion Transformers (DiT), it has been found in previous literature that DiT models tend to yield weaker features despite their stronger generation capability. This poses a threat to good generation-understanding unification. In this work, we show via controlled from-scratch training that long skip connections (LSCs) affect feature quality: a DiT with LSCs can produce better features. Furthermore, through detailed diagnosis, we reveal the mechanism causing this effect. Specifically, the input to a diffusion backbone contains both the latent image and the diffusion noise, where the diffusion noise, though appearing in the form of noises, actually reflects the information of the diffusion trajectory. To make the final prediction of a noisy variable ($v$ or $ε$), the diffusion backbone needs both signals. However, carrying both signals through the main backbone effectively "pollutes" the image signal with noises, leading to poor feature quality. In comparison, LSCs can shortcut diffusion noises directly to where they are needed, leaving much weaker noise signals in the main backbone, thus improving feature quality. To name the broader impact, this reveals that LSCs are not a mere trick but closely related to the diffusion objective. The code is at https://github.com/Darkbblue/dit-lsc.

title: CoGameReg: Cooperative-Game-Based Collaborative Semi-Supervised Regression for Seismic Reservoir Property Prediction
abstract: Accurate estimation of reservoir properties from seismic data remains challenging when well-log labels are sparse but three-dimensional seismic observations are abundant. We present CoGameReg, a cooperative-game-based semi-supervised regression framework that uses contribution-weighted predictions of heterogeneous regressors to construct shared pseudo-labels. This design makes each regressor's influence explicit in the learning targets generated for unlabeled seismic samples under sparse well control. The Tri-Game Shapley mechanism combines a rank-MSE performance game with a pairwise consistency game to estimate nonnegative regressor weights from labeled training data. These weights remain fixed during collaborative training and are reused for final prediction fusion. Candidate pseudo-labels are screened using a common local k-nearest-neighbor error-reduction criterion before retraining. We evaluate CoGameReg on 10 public regression datasets, a synthetic three-dimensional P-wave velocity prediction task, and a field water-saturation application. The benchmark advantage is most pronounced at the 2.5% labeled-data ratio and decreases as supervision increases. CoGameReg obtains the best blind-well metrics in the synthetic experiment. In the field application, predictions clipped to 0-100% yield a pooled coefficient of determination of 0.5942, a root mean square error of 5.7441 percentage points, and a Pearson correlation of 0.8265 across three blind wells. CoGameReg has the highest Pearson correlation among the four field methods. The results support the use of CoGameReg to integrate sparse well labels with dense seismic attributes, with performance varying across metrics and well locations.

title: Impacto de la inteligencia artificial en la optimización de la gestión de leads y la toma de decisiones comerciales en procesos de ventas digitales
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a strategic tool for optimizing sales management in digital sales environments. This study analyzed its impact on lead management, decision-making, objection handling, and sales closing in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). A quantitative, descriptive, non-experimental, and cross-sectional research design was employed. Data were collected through online surveys administered to 71 sales representatives and 15 executives, including sociodemographic questions, Likert-scale items, and open-ended questions. The results indicate the widespread use of digital tools to record and follow up on leads. Executives also recognize the strategic value of AI, although they identify limitations in the implementation of analytical mechanisms. It is concluded that AI enhances sales management; however, its impact depends on SMEs’ level of digital maturity, staff training, and the strengthening of technological capabilities.

title: Machine Learning–Based Predictive Model for Subscription Fraud Detection in the Telecommunication Sector of Adamawa State, Nigeria
abstract: This study presents the design and implementation of a machine learning–based fraud detection system for the telecommunications sector in Adamawa State, Nigeria. The existing system primarily stored raw subscriber data, including call detail records (CDRs) and user profiles, but lacked the predictive capability to proactively identify fraudulent activities. To address this limitation, a new model was developed incorporating data extraction, preprocessing, dataset creation, and behavioral as well as profile evaluation. Random Forest and Adaboost algorithms were applied to detect anomalies and patterns indicative of fraud, with Python serving as the main development environment. Subscriber data from 1,000 records, obtained through stratified random sampling, formed the training and validation dataset. title: Better together: Multi‐Agent system teamwork
abstract: Abstract While most present‐day multi‐agent system (MAS) deployments involve teams of agents within a single institution orchestrated by one or a few actors, some researchers are already beginning to appreciate the promise of more complex ecosystems consisting of hybrid human‐agent‐robot teams that operate across organizational and geographic boundaries. Importantly, effective teamwork does not emerge merely from making individual agents more capable or from accumulated experience working alongside other agents. Rather, success requires every essential ingredient to be present and planned for; failure requires only one to be missing. In addition to leveraging what is already known about team structure, heterogeneity/diversity, and team processes, research should also account for the diverse task types and forms of interdependence that make up sophisticated, performative joint activity in the real world. Considering the high‐stake opportunities and risks of MAS, a group of researchers from around the world have formed the international Multi‐Agent System Safety and Teamwork (MASST) initiative. Essays in this this AI Magazine special issue on Multi‐Agent System Teamwork—and its companion special issue on Multi‐Agent System Safety and Human‐Centered Agent Interaction—have been selected from the proceedings of past MASST events. In this article, we outline some of the needed requirements for making MAS “better together.” Innovative research relating to these requirements is grouped under four headings: 1. enabling scalable teamwork; 2. assuring multi‐agent alignment; 3. managing the nuanced dynamics of trust and delegation; 4. theory and design of “coordination‐first” systems

title: Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction for Signal Temporal Logic Inference with Many Classes
abstract: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) inference provides interpretable formulas for time series classification. For multiclass classification, however, accurate predictions do not necessarily ensure that the inferred formulas are satisfied consistently with the true class. We introduce the positive satisfaction rate and codeword satisfaction rate to quantify satisfaction of required formulas and consistency with the complete class codeword, respectively. We develop a two-stage procedure that first learns discriminative formulas using a margin-based objective and then refines predicate thresholds toward a small positive robustness target while fixing the formula structure and temporal intervals. Satisfaction and ranking penalties discourage violations of required formulas and loss of class separation. The decoding loss is used as a nonconformity score and calibrated separately for each class, providing finite-sample class-conditional coverage under intra-class exchangeability. Experiments on naval, synthetic, and robot manipulation trajectories demonstrate discrepancies between classification accuracy and formula satisfaction. The results further reveal a data-dependent tradeoff between robustness tightness and satisfaction, while class-conditional calibration mitigates undercoverage that can be hidden by pooled calibration.

title: Cost-Aware Iteration Allocation for Sequential Multi-Fidelity First-Order Optimization
abstract: Optimization can be expensive when evaluating the objective and its gradient requires a large dataset or a costly simulation. A cheaper approximation (i.e., a surrogate) can provide a useful initial point, but the work spent on that surrogate must be justified by the saving on the original problem. We study how many iterations to perform on each surrogate before switching to a more accurate objective. For a given sequence of smooth, strongly convex objectives, we use convergence bounds and distances between minimizers to construct a model of the total iteration cost. We derive closed-form two-level budgets for Nesterov's accelerated gradient method and a convex reformulation for multiple levels. We also develop an online switching rule that updates the cost comparison using the gradient at the current point. We test the techniques on a logistic-regression problem using HIGGS data. The online rule reduces weighted iteration cost in all 27 tested configurations, with a median cost of 52.8% of direct optimization. The results illustrate why updating the switching decision can be more effective than fixing the budget from an initial convergence bound.

title: Bicycle Race: small two-block codes on the Pareto frontier
abstract: Two-block group-algebra codes are among the simplest quantum LDPC codes, and many of them are translation invariant on a twisted torus, which suits neutral-atom arrays and other platforms with movable qubits. We ask how far they go at small sizes when searched systematically across all groups. We use algebraic constraints and screens to design a search pipeline capable of enumerating broad and complete swathes of two-block codes on a laptop. With it we census about $10^8$ two-block codes with up to $320$ qubits at check weights five to nine. Several of these censuses are exhaustive, and support complete statements; for instance, the Gross code is, up to equivalence, the only abelian weight-six two-block code with $n \le 200$ to reach $kd^2/n=12$, no weight-six two-block code with $n \le 300$ beats $[[288,16,16]]$, and the known $[[64,18,8]]$ is the best two-block code by $kd^2/n$ across weights five to nine with $n \le 94$. The censuses are also large enough to give insights into where good codes live - they concentrate in a handful of groups; abelian groups give the best codes at small $n$ and non-abelian groups at large $n$, with the crossover appearing to move out as the check weight grows; and high quality codes become $100$ to $1000$ times rarer per draw from weight six to weights eight and nine. Using the group algebra and the census data to steer a statistical search finds four to fifteen times as many good codes as uniform draws in equal time. Among the codes found are $[[102,20,10]]$ and $[[120,24,10]]$ at check weight nine, which we simulate in noisy syndrome-extraction circuits, and $[[186,20,18]]$, a weight-nine code with every check in a $5\times5$ window. At check weights seven to nine, our best codes exceed the best published $kd^2/n$ with exact distance at the same check weight in most length bands up to $320$ qubits. All codes are available in a public database.

title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

title: TestSuiteBench: Coding Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Test Suites from Specifications
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to create large software projects. While code-generation benchmarks have scaled accordingly to full applications, test-generation benchmarks remain limited to individual functions or bug fixes. In particular, generating complete test suites for complex software from scratch remains unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce TestSuiteBench, a benchmark of 165 open-source applications, each with a structured and detailed specification of intended behavior, a reference implementation, a reference test suite, and on average 74 mutants. Each mutant is generated from a single requirement of the specification and refined to isolate that behavior: 73\% are killed by exactly one reference test and, on average, by only 0.2\% of the remaining tests. We find that even frontier coding agents struggle to generate strong test suites given our specifications, achieving mutation scores below 60\%, despite their suites being largely valid and 88\% of their tests passing on the reference implementation. We observe that generated test suites often lack relevant input combinations and are smaller than reference test suites. Meanwhile, implementations generated for the same specifications pass 82\% of the reference tests. These results show agents can build software they cannot verify, a gap that directly limits fully autonomous software development.

title: HART: Hybrid Attention-RWKV Time series Foundation Model
abstract: Non-autoregressive multi-step forecasting (NAF) enables time series foundation models to predict an entire future horizon in a single forward pass. Despite its strong sequence modeling capabilities, RWKV-7 exhibits long-horizon degradation in our NAF experiments. In this setup, future patches are represented as missing inputs, requiring the recurrent state to evolve across the prediction horizon without new observations. Our analysis of RWKV-7's generalized delta rule suggests a mechanism we term Placeholder Idling Decay (PID): repeated state transitions can attenuate historical information when placeholder-driven writes provide insufficient compensation. Layer-wise analysis reveals reduced state-injection norms in most layers, while transition-matrix norms remain similar between historical and prediction regions, consistent with PID. Motivated by this analysis, we propose HART, a Hybrid Attention-RWKV Time-series Foundation Model that alternates attention and RWKV blocks, combining direct access to historical tokens with recurrent temporal modeling. Controlled experiments on GIFT-Eval and TIME-Benchmark show that HART improves over pure RWKV at medium and long horizons while maintaining comparable short-horizon performance, and achieves better aggregate performance than a comparably sized pure Transformer. With 36M parameters, HART achieves long-horizon MASE comparable to Toto-2.0-1B on GIFT-Eval (0.752 vs. 0.754), using approximately 1/28 of its parameters.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Ocular Surface Oncology: A Narrative Review of Multimodal Imaging, Smartphone-Based Screening, and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Ocular surface malignancies include ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), con-junctival melanoma, and conjunctival lymphoma. These rare disorders may threaten vi-sion and, in some cases, life. Early identification may be difficult because malignant le-sions can resemble benign ocular surface conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a potential aid to detection, classi-fication, and referral. This structured narrative review, organized with reference to SANRA principles, synthesizes PubMed/MEDLINE literature on AI applications in ocular surface oncology available through 29 August 2026. We examine slit-lamp photography, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and smartphone imaging. Deep-learning models have shown promising performance in selected binary OSSN tasks, whereas multiclass studies report lower sen-sitivity for rare malignancies such as conjunctival melanoma and lymphoma. Smartphone-based screening has also been evaluated in a prospective referral pathway, although the reference standard and verification process limit interpretation of popula-tion-level sensitivity. Dataset imbalance, image-acquisition variability, limited external and prospective validation, explainability, and workflow integration remain barriers to implementation. Future work should prioritize multicenter datasets, standardized acquisition, calibrated thresholds, and prospective human–AI evaluations. Current evidence supports further evaluation of AI as an adjunct for detection and referral, not as a re-placement for specialist assessment or histopathology.

title: Leveraging LiveKit for Real-Time AI-Driven Conversational Agents
abstract: Recent progress in real-time communication frameworks has significantly advanced the development of multimodal intelligent assistants that can interact with users in a natural, human-like manner.This paper introduces a LiveKit-based AI Assistant designed to enable seamless, low-latency human-computer interaction by integrating real-time audio streaming, large language model (LLM) reasoning, and automated system control within a unified architecture.The proposed framework utilizes LiveKit Agents for real-time connectivity, employs noise suppression plugins for robust speech processing, and leverages LangChain-based orchestration to ensure contextual understanding and reasoning [1], [2].In addition, the assistant incorporates a versatile toolkit for web-based search, voice-command interpretation, and operating system-level automation, enabling it to function effectively across diverse platforms and environments.Experimental evaluations indicate that the system achieves high responsiveness and scalability while maintaining lightweight deployment characteristics.Compared to existing conversational agents such as traditional virtual assistants, the proposed model offers superior customizability, cross-platform adaptability, and real-time feedback performance.This research underscores the potential of LiveKit-powered multimodal agents in shaping the future of real-time interactive AI systems suitable for both academic exploration and real-world deployment [3], [4].

title: Scalable neuromorphic photonic architecture based on nonlinear Si₃N₄ waveguides and neural network surrogate modeling
abstract: We present a scalable neuromorphic photonic computing architecture based on a χ⁽³⁾ silicon nitride waveguide. Using three-dimensional FDTD simulation, we characterize nonlinear mode coupling across 15 guided modes and verify linear scaling of the nonlinear field difference across four propagation lengths — 12.5, 25, 50, and 100 micrometers — confirming Kerr nonlinear accumulation consistent with theory. Simulation cost is minimized through length-nonlinearity equivalence scaling, reducing all production runs to the 12.5 μm geometry. A dataset of input mode combinations and corresponding output mode coefficients — extracted via modal decomposition at the output facet — trains a neural network surrogate that replaces expensive FDTD evaluations during optimization. The S-matrix formalism describes the inverse design region, enabling gradient-based joint optimization of input modes and waveguide geometry. Each waveguide-plus-inverse-design pair acts as a cascadable physical neural network layer, forming a scalable architecture for mode conversion, multiplexing, and neuromorphic optical computing.

title: Competitive scaling of small-subsystem-optimization heuristics for LABS
abstract: The low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) problem, often formulated as a spin-lattice energy-minimization problem, is a combinatorial optimization problem with a very rugged energy landscape. We demonstrate that iterative optimization of very small subsystems of n spins that are decoupled from the rest of the system achieves global optimization of LABS with a time-to-solution scaling that is competitive with heuristics that optimize the global system of N spins directly. Our isolated-subsystem heuristic with n = 4 achieves a time scaling of O(1.333^N ) on the interval N = [27, 60], while the current state-of-the-art classical and quantum scalings are respectively O(1.34^N ) and O(1.21^N ). Our results suggest that specialized optimization hardware with only small numbers of logical spins may be of practical relevance.

title: Axiom-0: Hierarchical Self-Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Reliable manipulation requires policies that generalize across tasks, layouts, and object interactions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained multimodal understanding with learned control, but their performance remains limited on unfamiliar task compositions. We present Axiom-0, a VLA policy that addresses both the quality of its representations and their use in action generation through hierarchical self-refinement. Intra-VLM Representation Refinement (IVRR) strengthens selected intermediate features through consistency supervision with learned feature projections during training. VLM-Action Interface Refinement (VAIR) recursively updates the resulting conditioning before action generation. Joint optimization of the supervised VLM layers, VAIR, and the action generator connects the two components. On RoboCasa365, Axiom-0 achieves 62.32% overall success in our evaluation, exceeding the highest published leaderboard score (Paimon-0, 58.1%) by 4.22 percentage points and the Xiaomi-Robotics-1 reference by 4.92 points. Under the evaluated profiling setup, mean action-chunk generation latency increases by 1.7% over Xiaomi-Robotics-1. These results demonstrate improved task completion with modest inference overhead.

title: CorrFlow: Exact and Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching on the Correlation Elliptope
abstract: Correlation matrices combine nonlinear positive-definiteness constraints with a simultaneous row-column permutation symmetry. Their generation therefore involves two distinct problems. First, every output must remain on the correlation elliptope, irrespective of how its variables are ordered. Second, the generator must learn the domain-specific distribution occupied by empirical data inside that valid space. Existing financial image generators mix these problems: they learn ordered matrix entries and repair invalid draws afterward. We introduce CorrFlow, which separates them. A generalized Fisher transform maps full-rank correlation matrices bijectively to unconstrained coordinates, guaranteeing valid outputs without projection. A graph flow-matching network learns the empirical distribution in those coordinates and is permutation equivariant: reordering the variables only reorders the output. We compare a conditional CorrGAN reimplementation, image diffusion, and CorrFlow on $80\times80$ Taiwan equity matrices using five seeds per neural method. CorrFlow produces 100% valid draws without repair and obtains feature sliced-Wasserstein distance $.712\pm.141$, versus $4.339\pm.252$ for CorrGAN and $4.610\pm.191$ for image diffusion after their invalid outputs are projected back to the correlation space. It also improves this distance over historical lookup, while lookup retains higher local coverage. These results support the combined construction under the evaluated training budget; they do not establish superiority over fully tuned image models or isolate the contribution of each component.

title: Phonology-Aware Speaker Extraction Frontend for Audio LLMs
abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) is a key frontend for enabling audio large language models (LLMs) to recognize and understand a designated speaker in overlapping speech. However, multilingual mixtures exhibit heterogeneous extraction demands, causing fixed-depth systems to either under-process challenging inputs or waste computation on inputs that have already converged. Existing TSE frontends generally apply uniform computation, while Audio-LLM adaptation methods neither explicitly model language-conditioned extraction demands nor preserve plug-and-play compatibility with frozen downstream models. We therefore propose LATTE, a lightweight 5.2M-parameter frontend that combines an acoustic Difficulty Estimator, a task-adaptive phonology-informed prior learned from multi-depth TSE gains, and an Adaptive Hourglass Extractor to route each mixture without requiring language identity at inference. On PolyExtract, LATTE achieves a macro SI-SNRi of 15.07 dB at 0.30 GFLOPs, retaining performance within 0.09 dB of a 0.53-GFLOP fixed-depth model while reducing computation by 43.4%, and lowers the average WER from 16.8% to 14.6% relative to TF-GridNet. By jointly modeling sample-level extraction demands and phonological structure, LATTE provides a practical framework for quality-aware, compute-efficient multilingual TSE and offers a scalable path toward robust Audio-LLM deployment.
