title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction
abstract: Diagnostic information in multi-view medical imaging studies, like echocardiography, is distributed across views, each capturing different aspects of cardiac structure and function. In clinical practice, these views are first interpreted through quantitative measurements, which then support specific diagnoses. However, existing echo representation learning methods do not explicitly model measurements as an intermediate representation between views and diagnosis. As a result, individual measurements are not explicitly represented in a form that downstream diagnostic tasks can selectively use, hindering accurate diagnosis. Inspired by this hierarchical clinical workflow, we introduce EchoTab, a measurement-grounded representation learning framework that represents multi-view echocardiography studies using measurement-specific tokens as an intermediate representation between echo views and diagnosis. Each measurement token selectively attends to the views relevant to its estimation and is trained through tabular reconstruction to predict the corresponding measurement value. The resulting tokens form a factorized echo representation, which encode clinically meaningful structural and functional properties and can be selectively used for downstream diagnosis. Unlike the commonly used contrastive approaches, EchoTab does not require negative samples or large batch sizes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that EchoTab learns effective measurement-grounded representations that improve diagnosis classification in multi-view echocardiography and its learned attention aligns with established measurement-view relationships used by cardiologists. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/michelleespranita/EchoTab.

title: DuoRate: Two-Rate Per-Expert Precision Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Serving
abstract: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store-read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. Online, it profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate-distortion allocation under the decode functional; routing frequency provably cancels from every per-expert decision, and the solve costs one dot product per expert and a bisection. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, DuoRate reading 2.3 bpw exceeds every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4-1.6 bpw more. The advantage is largest under long decoding: on GSM8K, DuoRate at 2.9 bpw matches or exceeds every 4-bit format and trails BF16 by only 0.25 points, and at 2.6 bpw it still matches or exceeds the 4.5-bit NF4 and FP4. Against controls in its own format, the allocation alone is worth 0.07-0.11 bpw of read rate. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Localized Generative Design of Ship Hulls with Diffusion Models and High-Fidelity Assessment
abstract: Practical ship design requires localized refinement and performance evaluation. This paper presents a reward-directed diffusion framework for localized hull optimization. Parametric masking during dataset generation restricts geometric changes to selected variables, including the bulbous bow and forebody, while preserving full-hull continuity. Surrogate-assisted sequential Monte Carlo sampling targets reduced predicted calm-water resistance, with stability retained through training data and displacement matched during screening. An automated viscous free-surface CFD pipeline, validated against measurements for two benchmark container ships, evaluates a generated variant and GenHull E, a hull refined by a naval architect within the same representation. At matched KRISO Container Ship (KCS) displacement, the generated variant has comparable total resistance at $F_n=0.195$ but 45-50% higher resistance at $F_n=0.250$ and $0.260$, missed by empirical screening. GenHull E achieves 6-8% lower total resistance up to $F_n=0.240$ but higher resistance above $F_n=0.250$ as opposing friction and pressure trends reverse the gains. Aggregating resistance across this crossover can conceal tradeoffs that emerge when friction and pressure components are evaluated separately. The assessment reveals an inability to represent a faired bulbous bow and a reward lacking viscous pressure and stability terms. These findings show how high-fidelity assessment informs improved representations and objectives for physically realizable generative designs.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions of Artificial Intelligence in Mortgage Lending
abstract: The mortgage lending industry is experiencing a significant transformation as it embraces Artificial Intelligence (AI) for its impact on decision-making, operations, risk management, and customer service. Many of the activities associated with mortgage processes can be automated and improved using technologies such as ML, DL, NLP, computer vision and generative AI, as these tasks are often document-driven, rule-based, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on manual work. Credit risk assessment, automated underwriting, fraud detection, intelligent document processing, property valuation, default prediction, mortgage servicing and customer support are just some of the ways AI is being applied to the credit industry. The study also identifies trends that are emerging such as explainable and agentic AI systems, which could help in making better mortgage decisions. But there are several challenges with the implementation of AI, including data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic bias, poor data quality, regulatory compliance, unreliable model performance amidst shifting market dynamics, and others. There are future developments anticipated in explainable and responsible AI, privacy-preserving learning, generative and multimodal AI, adaptive governance, and more human-AI collaboration. In summary, if implemented appropriately, AI can enhance mortgage lending processes by making them more efficient and intelligent, while ensuring transparency, fairness, security, and good governance.

title: Who gets the information? An alpha-fair label-coverage framework for multi-label feature selection
abstract: Information-theoretic filters are popular for multi-label feature selection, yet recent criteria disagree on how to distribute relevance over labels: some amplify features that inform a few labels, others balance the information every label receives. We show that these choices are implicit social welfare functions. Treating labels as agents whose utility is the information delivered by the selected features, we propose FLIC (Fair Label-Information Coverage), which greedily maximises the α-fair welfare of per-label information coverage. A single parameter α moves from utilitarian (α=0) through proportionally fair (α=1) to max-min selection (α→∞), and the relevance terms of a dozen published filters are recovered as special cases, first-order approximations or limits. The objective is monotone submodular for every α≥0 whenever each label's information is, so greedy selection is a (1-1/e)-approximation; this fails for α<0, and the max-min limit is inapproximable. Fano's and the Hellman-Raviv inequalities tie raw coverage to the Bayes Hamming loss and normalised coverage to each label's relative error. FLIC uses bias-corrected, label-wise conditional information, needs no relevance-redundancy trade-off parameter and runs in O(knqd) time. On 22 data sets, with all choices fixed on separate development data, FLIC has the best average rank among 14 information-theoretic filters on seven of nine metrics. Against three tuned embedded methods neither side dominates: FLIC ranks first on ranking loss, coverage and macro-AUC, the embedded methods on Hamming loss, one-error and micro-F1. An α-sweep confirms the predicted trade-off between Hamming loss and macro-averaged metrics. Preprint of a manuscript submitted to Pattern Recognition (Elsevier) on October 8, 2026; currently under review.

title: Dataset-Calibrated Perturbation Budgets for Adversarial Robustness Evaluation of Machine-Learning Network Intrusion Detection Systems
abstract: Adversarial evaluation of machine-learning-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDSs) requires an explicit bound on attacker perturbations, yet fixed bounds are often reused across datasets without verifying scale comparability. We evaluate two differentiable detectors on CICIDS2017, TON_IoT, and UNSW-NB15 using a constrained, control-surface-aware evasion procedure in which perturbation cost is measured in interquartile-range units. The measured constrained feature-space evasion cost differs by more than two orders of magnitude across benchmarks. On UNSW-NB15, changing only the perturbation bound from a fixed reference value of 50 to a dataset-calibrated P95 value changes measured evasion success from 2.6% to 84.0%, with the conclusion remaining stable across P90, P95, and P99 calibration. We therefore propose a dataset-specific quantile calibration procedure and a monotonicity-based internal validity test exploiting nested attacker action spaces. Calibration removes the severe fixed-bound monotonicity violations observed on the two most poorly scaled datasets, although the test remains diagnostic rather than certifying. A secondary attribution-based robustness estimator does not generalise consistently across the three benchmarks. These results show that perturbation-budget calibration is an essential component of credible cross-dataset adversarial NIDS evaluation.

abstract: Актуальность исследования обусловлена потребностью в локальном голосовом управлении ПК без передачи речевых данных во внешние службы. title: Beyond Discrepancy: Oracle Drift in Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization
abstract: We analyze distributional drift in nonstationary weighted risk minimization by decomposing the excess risk into estimation, drift, and approximation components. The drift error is commonly bounded through discrepancy-type quantities that control changes of the risk over classes of predictors. We instead relate the drift error directly to the movement of the best predictor within the model class and analyze its behavior in parametrized regression models. Our analysis shows that discrepancy-type quantities can be overly conservative: unlike our oracle drift, they may scale at a larger order than the resulting excess-risk contribution and can respond to changes in the risk surface that do not affect the optimal predictor. For linear regression, we characterize this gap sharply and combine the resulting drift bounds with estimation guarantees. We further extend the analysis to nonparametric regression.

title: Taking Tokenization off the Host for Agentic LLM Serving
abstract: Agentic workloads resend long contexts that barely change between calls. Prefix caching now skips most of their prefill, yet every request must still be tokenized in full before the cache can even be consulted. Tokenization, a CPU stage long treated as negligible, becomes the largest part of time-to-first-token (TTFT), and a frontend that tokenizes for a whole GPU fleet limits how many GPUs it can feed. We present GraphTok, a GPU tokenizer that runs the entire encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, as one replayable CUDA graph. GraphTok reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit on GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo. GraphTok encodes one million GPT-2 tokens in 1.7-3.2 ms including data transfers, and on Llama 3 it is 4.7-6.0x faster than gigatoken, the strongest CPU tokenizer. On TokTier's own single-request benchmark, it is 2.6-3.9x faster than gigatoken and up to 18.1x faster than TokTier. In vLLM with a cached prefix, it lowers mean TTFT by 2.1-2.4x. The largest gain is capacity. Within a 2 s P99 target, one Dynamo frontend with GraphTok sustains 518 requests/s of 121k-token traffic, the busiest-hour load of 56 GPUs, against 296 with gigatoken and 18.5 with the default tokenizer. Across 121k to one million tokens, this is 1.75-2.5x the load gigatoken sustains, with a P99 up to 64x lower where gigatoken's tail breaks.

title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{κ+o(1)}$, for any fixed $κ>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = Ω(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+ω(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.

title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
abstract: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.

title: Selective Spatio-Temporal Fruit Inspector (S$^2$FI): A Mamba-based Framework for Rotational Fruit Quality Assessment
abstract: The global fruit and vegetable industry confronts severe post-harvest sorting challenges for small and medium-scale growers. Large intelligent sorting systems are too costly, while manual sorting suffers from low efficiency, inconsistent standards, and high labor demand. To bridge this gap between expensive equipment and inefficient manual work, this study develops a low-cost, high-efficiency, lightweight fruit sorting system driven by deep learning, suitable for small and medium growers. We propose the Selective Spatio-Temporal Fruit Inspector (S$^2$FI) architecture, which combines a 3D convolutional encoder with a Mamba-based backbone.It efficiently extracts spatiotemporal features, adaptively weighs informative frames during fruit rotation, and models long-range dependencies with linear complexity, reducing motion blur and occlusion. The hardware uses a dual-conveyor and curved rail design, supporting household power, fast deployment, and lightweight embedded deployment to improve affordability. We also built a conveyor-based fruit quality video dataset with 6,460 samples. Experiments on the held-out test set show that our method achieves the best trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and practicality, outperforming the compared baselines on the test set, achieving an excellent balance of accuracy, speed, and practicality for real-world sorting.

title: Literal Integrity Is Not Semantic Integrity: Descriptive Records Re-anchor Unchanged Commands
abstract: AI agents turn natural-language commands into physical and digital actions. Their safeguards check the literal command: sender, integrity, and absence of competing instructions. All can pass while the action is wrong. Records that only describe past events, with no instruction or definition, change an unchanged command’s meaning: after logged lock requests answered by unlocking, a model unlocks the door. We call this semantic re-anchoring and set one safety goal: only the owner’s own channel may change a command’s meaning. Across languages, model families, and endpoints from stated meaning to executed tool call, every tested model fails somewhere. Resistance is not immunity: models that never reverse a pair still flip single commands, and unauthorized tool calls run far higher. One record can reverse a command; the reversal reaches unseen synonyms, survives one explicit malfunction warning, and enters through tool output. Claimed or forged owner approval is treated as authoritative, by some models on every command. Stated meaning does not predict action, even with reasoning on. The effect generalizes beyond the word, and literal checks miss it: detectors, precedence rules, delimiting and action checks each leave a path open in some tested model. Semantic integrity must be enforced where commands become actions.

title: Phase records control the conversion cost of non-Gaussian light
abstract: Detecting non-Gaussian light establishes that a resource is present. Its structure and preparation record determine the cost of turning it into a specified output. This paper gives matching conversion-cost laws for weak optical sources and a general input certificate that can exclude every allowed Gaussian receiver before a circuit is designed. title: Architecture Design and Resource Scheduling
abstract: In response to the contradiction between large-scale teaching and personalized needs in the digital transformation of ideological and political theory courses in universities, as well as the problems of lagging response and low resource scheduling efficiency in existing intelligent education systems in high concurrency scenarios, this paper designs and implements an AI empowered intelligent teaching system based on micro-service architecture. The system adopts a layered architecture design, deeply integrating natural language processing, knowledge graph and retrieval enhanced generation technologies, and realizing core functions such as intelligent content analysis, personalized learning recommendation, and intelligent question answering assistant. This study provides a complete technical solution from architecture design to algorithm optimization for intelligent teaching of ideological and political courses in universities, which has high promotional value.

title: THE ROLE OF AI TECHNOLOGY IN MAMMOGRAPHIC SCREENING OF BREAST CANCER WITH EVALUATION OF EFFICIENCY AND POTENTIAL FOR PRACTICAL HEALTH CARE
abstract: In conditions of increasing workload on organized mammographic screening programs and deficiency of qualified personnel, implementation of auxiliary technologies on the basis of artificial intelligence (AI) acquires special actuality. The results of retrospective cohort study included 100 histologically verified cases of breast cancer (BI-RADS category 6) permitted to evaluate diagnostic efficiency of AI algorithm as compared to independent conclusions of three certified radiologists with length of service more than 10 years. The sensitivity of technology of AI amounted 86%-96%, depending on dichotomization model. The percentage of total coincidence with appraisal of experts varied within the limits 87-91%. The level of concordance, assessed using weighted Cohen's kappa coefficient, came up to κq = 0.76 (95% CI: 0.68-0.83) that corresponds to "good" concordance. In 1%-3% of cases, the AI algorithm identified suspicious findings missed by experts, at that without increasing volume of groundless examinations due to conservative classification of most disputable cases as BI-RADS 3 with ordering dynamic observation. The obtained results confirm clinical applicability of AI technology as standardizing and relieving tool in practical health care, capable to increase sensitivity of screening and to decrease risk of false-negative conclusions without violation of established clinical protocols.

title: Using JA4+ Fingerprints for Device Identification in Encrypted IoT Networks
abstract: This paper investigates whether JA4+ fingerprint decomposition improves passive identification of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in encrypted network environments, without incorporating payload inspection or active probing techniques. As TLS encryption and privacy-preserving mechanisms such as Encrypted Client Hello reduce the visibility of application-layer metadata, traditional payload- and domain-based identification techniques become less effective. JA4+ fingerprints provide an alternative approach by extracting observable characteristics from TLS handshakes, certificates, and transport-layer metadata without requiring traffic decryption. The proposed methodology evaluates different JA4+ fingerprint combinations for IoT device identification using traffic traces from the CICIoT2023 dataset, with additional validation on the UNSW-IoTraffic dataset. Traffic traces were processed with Zeek to extract the JA4+ fingerprint family, which was evaluated using dictionary-based classification, Random Forest, and Categorical Boosting models. Compact fingerprint representations were compared with decomposed protocol-level features to determine whether feature decomposition improves classification performance or enhances interpretability. Experimental results show that JA4+ fingerprints enable accurate IoT device identification using only passive encrypted traffic metadata. On CICIoT2023, the complete JA4+* configuration achieved a Macro F1-score of 0.8095 with both RF and CatBoost, although this result was obtained on a smaller subset of connections due to fingerprint availability. On the independent UNSW-IoTraffic dataset, CatBoost achieved a Macro F1-score of 0.9995 with both compact and decomposed representations. Overall, decomposed representations did not provide a consistent predictive advantage over compact fingerprints, although they remained valuable for interpretability and feature-level analysis. These findings indicate that compact JA4+ fingerprints can preserve the discriminative information required for IoT device identification without requiring protocol-level decomposition when predictive performance is the primary objective. The results highlight the potential of JA4+ fingerprinting for scalable IoT security monitoring under increasingly encrypted network conditions.

title: Entropy-preserving linear unit (EPLU): a robust activation function for stable and efficient training of deep neural networks
abstract: Activation functions or the nonlinearity play a fundamental role in deep neural networks (NN) by governing gradient propagation, preventing neuron saturation and collapse, and preserving information flow across network layers. Since small changes in activation can greatly affect neural network performance, it is important to explore new activation functions and evaluate their potential impact. While widely used functions such as ReLU, Swish, and GELU have achieved remarkable empirical success, they often suffer from limitations including gradient instability, dead neurons, and suboptimal performance when applied to modern architectures such as vision transformers. Furthermore, the rapid evolution of deep learning models necessitates the development of adaptive activation functions that generalize effectively across diverse architectures. To address these challenges, we propose a novel activation function termed the Entropy-Preserving Linear Unit (EPLU), designed to maintain representational entropy, improve gradient flow, and enhance training robustness in deep networks. EPLU introduces a smooth, adaptive nonlinearity that mitigates saturation effects while preserving critical information throughout the network hierarchy. We evaluated EPLU within transformer-based architectures across multiple object recognition benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-200. Experimental results demonstrate that EPLU consistently outperforms state-of-the-art activation functions, including ReLU, Swish, and GELU, achieving 1~2% improvements in classification accuracy. Furthermore, detailed analysis of training dynamics reveals that EPLU maintains more stable gradient norms, leading to improved convergence behavior and enhanced training robustness. These results highlight EPLU as a promising activation function for next-generation deep learning models, particularly in transformer-based architectures, offering superior performance, stability, and generalization.

title: Decentralized Bandit Learning of Markov Perfect Equilibria
abstract: We study decentralized bandit learning in discounted infinite-horizon, general-sum Markov games with continuous actions. Agents observe the public state, but only their own realized rewards, and use simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation to update their actions. Under strong monotonicity of the negative running-reward gradients and sufficiently small time steps, we prove that the fully decentralized procedure converges almost surely to the unique stationary Markov perfect equilibrium. We obtain an $O(n^{-1/2})$ convergence rate and present a natural extension to episodic finite-horizon learning.

title: CoVA: Composing VAE Representations for Generative Learning
abstract: Representation alignment with pretrained visual encoders improves diffusion transformer training but requires auxiliary encoders and extra training overhead. Recent approaches instead exploit representations from the generative model's own variational autoencoder (VAE). However, reconstruction-oriented VAE features are not optimized for the semantic discrimination and spatial structure needed for generative learning. We introduce \textbf{CoVA} (\textbf{Co}mposed \textbf{VA}E Representations), a lightweight framework that composes VAE features online into stage-wise guidance for flow-matching training. A small latent composer is jointly trained with class supervision, masked latent reconstruction, and horizontal-flip consistency, yielding semantically discriminative, spatially structured dense features and sample-dependent class posteriors. CoVA aligns intermediate SiT features with the composed representations early in training, then removes the increasingly detrimental alignment and reuses detached composer posteriors for sample-dependent soft label conditioning. We further uncover a hidden confound in soft label conditioning: averaging class embeddings attenuates their magnitude, coupling semantic interpolation with conditioning strength. This attenuation alone can substantially improve FID while degrading Recall, revealing a non-semantic source of the apparent gain. CoVA corrects this confound by restoring the hard-label magnitude, isolating posterior-dependent directional semantics. CoVA adds only 8.5M training-only auxiliary parameters (1.3\% of SiT-XL/2) and introduces no inference-time overhead. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, CoVA reduces SiT-XL/2 FID from 17.2 to 7.4 (\textbf{57\%}) in 400K steps. With classifier-free guidance, it achieves an FID of \textbf{2.03} in only 400 epochs, versus 2.06 after 1,400 epochs for vanilla SiT-XL/2.

title: Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.

title: CaptchaAgent: Verifiable Visual Reasoning for CAPTCHA Solving
abstract: Modern reasoning CAPTCHAs require fine-grained perception, compositional relation reasoning, and grounded browser interaction. End-to-end vision-language model agents remain brittle in this setting because a missed object, incorrect count, or confused relation can propagate directly to the final action. To address this problem, we present CaptchaAgent, a structured visual reasoning framework for interactive CAPTCHA solving. Instead of predicting an action directly from a screenshot, CaptchaAgent first constructs a visual intermediate representation (V-IR) that explicitly records entities, attributes, and spatial or topological relations. A symbol-only ASCII protocol further requires the parser to commit to a concrete object set and count. Building on this global representation, localized evidence refinement revisits ambiguous regions at higher effective resolution, while counterfactual consistency verification tests whether the resulting action remains stable under task-preserving transformations. Across three proprietary backbones on Open CaptchaWorld, CaptchaAgent improves Pass@1 by 21.3-25.8 percentage points over a commercially available browser agent baseline evaluated with the same backbones. On the separate offline Oedipus-data benchmark, it further improves average Pass@1 by 9.2-12.3 percentage points over the Oedipus solver across three matched backbones. The intermediate traces show that exact counting, continuous geometry, and ordered execution remain major sources of automation difficulty for the evaluated agents, providing practical guidance for designing more resilient compositional CAPTCHAs.

title: A pair-primary associative substrate with exact in-band episodic memory
abstract: We build a GPU-resident associative memory whose unit of representation is a relation: an ordered word pair with a signed binding strength, in place of the token. One rule drives all writes. On each exposure the binding state moves a fixed fraction of the way toward a ceiling that the world asserts. The rule admits an exact in-band episodic trace. Each binding carries six accumulators with distinct decay rates; together they form a sufficient statistic for the binding's exposure history. The ordered sequence of asserted targets follows by inverting the resulting generalized Vandermonde system. Count recovers exactly on all 4,640 live bindings (the complete live web, not a sample). Order recovers on the production bank to 1.5e-10 in float64 at depth six (2.4e-13 at depth three), and to 1.2e-3 through the production float32 kernels at four-step histories. The exactness claim is conditional: at least as many distinct, well-separated rates as history depth, and precision exceeding the conditioning (section 3.5). Those conditions collapse to one law, error ≈ ratio × cond(V) × precision (median ratio 0.03-0.05 over a six-order-of-magnitude sweep), so a unit's exactness envelope is computable before it is built (section 3.6). The rate set follows by minimizing cond(V), 867× better-conditioned than the reference (section 3.7). Pairing two rate bands lifts the exact depth from six to nine in float64, past the M ≥ k count wall (section 3.8). A shared-state control runs the identical law in a linear-attention layout. One binding alone on a shared state recovers exactly; at one thousand shared pairs the worst pair errs at 1.7e3 while the pair-primary arm holds at 1e-12 across all populations. The write-landing site, not the read geometry, carries the difference. Replaying the recorded input ledger rebuilds 9,272 of 9,296 nonzero live bindings, 99.7 percent. The two theorems supply state-only inversion for the organ-backed quantities, count and order.

title: Code and results for "Similarity-Metric Sensitivity in Hard and Soft Clustering" (v1.0)
abstract: Code, per-trial results, and figures for the article "Similarity-Metric Sensitivity in Hard and Soft Clustering: A Statistically Grounded Comparison of K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, and K-Nearest Neighbors, with a Mineral-Composition Case Study" (A. V. Shinde, D. D. Patil, B. A. Ahire, S. S. Bhavsar; submitted to Results in Engineering, 2026). The Python pipeline compares K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, and a supervised KNN reference under the Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, and Pearson metrics. Each metric uses a matched estimator (spherical k-means, correlation clustering, k-medians, fuzzy c-medians), and all metrics run on the same standardised features. It covers Iris, Wine, WDBC, and a de-circularised synthetic mineral-composition dataset, with 30 bootstrap-resampled trials per configuration. Included: the experiment and statistics scripts (two-way ANOVA, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests, pooled variance partition, TOST equivalence tests), the per-trial results, the generated LaTeX tables, and all figures. All randomness is seeded and the stored results are reproduced exactly. See README.md for the run order.

title: Information Provenance and Conservative Enrichment in Prospective Health
abstract: Description Prospective Health evaluates present organizational realization together with the adequacy of lawful, constitutively viable continuations under declared conditions. This fourth paper in the Health, Formally Defined series establishes a machine-checked finite benchmark for examining how information enters, survives, and is transformed throughout that measurement architecture. A five-state forest system provides a complete formal setting in which contextual admissibility, constitutive continuation, response observation, capacity representation, and Health judgments can be examined exhaustively. Two equivalent history encodings establish invariance under relocating contextual restrictions between dependent history constructors and an explicit lawfulness predicate. The resulting candidate–lawful–viable response pipeline identifies the precise contribution of each semantic filter. The benchmark establishes an exact information-refinement ladder with five detailed-response classes, four original-capacity classes, and three classes distinguished by the complete declared Health language. Machine-checked classification results identify every distinction lost through representational compression and every additional distinction retained by capacity but unused by the established Health queries. A general conservative-capacity-refinement lemma gives sufficient conditions for preserving existing Health judgments under representational enrichment. A strict forest instance demonstrates how additional response information can support new queries while preserving established adequacy through exact projection. The results establish a formally verified reference for information provenance, observation sufficiency, and conservative evolution of Health representations. Their scope is the declared finite dynamics and set-valued capacity semantics. Extensions to probability-weighted capacity require compatible stochastic laws and preservation of query-relevant events. The companion empirical-synthetic measurement study investigates these additional obligations under incomplete ecological observations, uncertain dynamics, and numerical inference.

title: Reward-Quality Divergence (RQD): Code, Saved Runs and Analysis Scripts (Anonymous Review Artifact)
abstract: Anonymous review artifact for the paper Reward-Quality Divergence: Telling Judge Gaming from Judge Error in Visual RL. Please do not try to identify the authors. RQD measures the gap between a judge's reward and an anchor-based quality score during reinforcement learning, subtracts the gap that exists before training (the floor), and labels the remaining gap growth as gaming, drift, collapse or none. Contents Code: the measure, the anchor checker, the judge wrapper with its prompt, the control rewards, the second grader and the re-scoring job. Results: the saved answers, rewards and anchor scores of all 154 training runs reported in the paper, plus the re-scoring and second-grader results. Analysis scripts: CPU-only scripts that rebuild every table of the paper from the saved results in a few minutes. Data: item files with the question, reference answer and anchor fact of every item (no images; the images come from the public ChartQA, GQA and DocVQA datasets). Human labels: the 100 human correctness labels used to check the anchor. Checks included: one script recomputes the anchor score of all 219,500 saved answers from the item files and the released checker and compares it with the stored score; unit tests cover the measure, the anchor and the rewards. The GRPO training loop and the cluster job scripts are not part of this review artifact; they will be released with the published paper. All training settings are listed in the paper's appendix. Code: MIT license. Result files and human labels: CC BY 4.0. The datasets keep their original licenses. See README.md for the commands.

title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations: supporting data
abstract: Supporting research data for physical-state supervision of design-only Gaussian process surrogates, with optional mixture-of-experts comparisons. Includes 1,987 CH designs, 3,000 thermal-explosion designs, 3,000 recalculated Be/Cocktail designs, state diagnostics, saved predictions, paired evaluation metrics, learning curves, grid diagnostics, timing records and file-level provenance. The data record does not include software, solver binaries, material libraries or raw trajectories. Grid sensitivities and historical reproduction limitations are documented in README.md. title: Adaptive Group Feature Stream Selection for Dynamic Feature Stream
abstract: Feature selection is a dimensionality reduction technique that identifies relevant features while discarding irrelevant and redundant ones. Traditional feature selection methods require the entire feature space to be known in advance, making them suitable for static datasets. However, in real-world applications such as healthcare monitoring, sensor networks, and image analysis, new features are generated at different time intervals. In dynamic feature streams, the entire feature space is not known beforehand. To address this challenge, this paper proposes Adaptive Group Feature Stream Selection (AGFS), an online feature selection framework for dynamic feature streams. The proposed framework extends the Alpha-Investing algorithm from processing features individually to processing features that arrive in randomly sized groups. It employs a multi-stage processing approach. First, variance filtering removes constant features. Next, Alpha-Investing-based statistical testing selects relevant feature groups. A group-size capping mechanism is introduced to prevent larger feature groups from being discarded during statistical testing. Within each selected group, features are ranked using feature-class correlation, and redundant features are removed using correlation-based redundancy removal. A data-driven threshold, computed from feature-class correlation observed so far, is introduced to help prevent unnecessary elimination of complementary features. An adaptive wealth mechanism rewards the selection of informative features. Experiments conducted on six benchmark datasets using a K-Nearest Neighbours classifier with 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves higher average classification accuracy (87.36%) while maintaining a competitive number of selected features compared to existing feature selection methods. The proposed approach is also validated across multiple classifiers and its consistency across classifiers is reported.

title: AI and Corporate Strategy: HorizonAI
abstract: Business strategy has evolved dramatically over the past century. Applying new and improved organizational and strategic methodologies in tandem with AI reshapes strategy by providing actionable intelligence across the three domains of leadership. In this chapter, the authors begin with the horizon scanning/scenario planning component of strategic fitness, with organizational excellence and growth creation. In the past, scenario planning was restricted to strategy and R&D offices. HorizonAI is a structured framework blending human strategic foresight with AI's analytical muscle. It consists of four steps: Observe, Attack, Orient, and Adapt (OAOA). AI is revolutionizing scenario planning by transforming what was once a lengthy, periodic exercise into a continuous, data-driven process. To institutionalize adaptation, many firms now embed AI into executive decision meetings. AI is the enabler, not the replacement, for human strategic foresight.

title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
abstract: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than optimising low-step updates directly, TraceSampler models endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes high-dimensional error predictable from the sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24$\times$ fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.

title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
abstract: Web crawling is a major source of large language model (LLM) pretraining data, yet data-selection pipelines discard a large share of crawled pages. We investigate how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts to collect more high-quality pretraining data. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host crawl coverage, we find that roughly half of the variation in classifier scores occurs between hosts. In the crawls we analyze, a few pages from a host also provide a useful estimate of the quality of its remaining pages. Common Crawl uses harmonic centrality, a graph centrality metric, to guide its crawl allocation. In our simulations, using centrality to choose which hosts to crawl yields limited gains over random ordering and performs worse for some classifiers. For deciding how deeply to crawl each host, sampling a few pages and then fetching more from hosts with higher-scoring samples collects several times more high-quality pages per fetch than uniform depth or centrality-based allocation. Finally, Common Crawl's observed per-host coverage has little correlation with the evaluated quality signals. We estimate that tens of millions of high-quality pages remain among known but uncrawled URLs in each crawl examined, with most concentrated on a small share of hosts.

title: Robust Langevin Sampling under State-Dependent Heavy-Tailed Noise with Applications to LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Existing convergence guarantees for non-log-concave sampling with stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo (SG-LMC) typically assume globally Lipschitz gradients and uniformly bounded noise variance. Both assumptions can fail even in elementary sampling problems, and relaxing them better reflects practical applications such as Bayesian fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). We relax both assumptions through generalized smoothness and our proposed state-dependent heavy-tailed oracle with finite $p$-th moments, $1<p\leq 2$. The oracle permits infinite variance when $p<2$ and includes the Blum-Gladyshev (BG-0) condition. We study these relaxations separately and jointly, proposing three methods. Under globally Lipschitz gradients, robust LMC (R-LMC) handles the proposed oracle through geometric-median centering and residual clipping. With exact gradients, adaptive LMC (A-LMC) controls discretization error under generalized smoothness. Robust adaptive LMC (RA-LMC) addresses both relaxations through robust estimation and a noise-aware step size. For all three methods, we establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees in Fisher information (FI) without assuming dissipativity or a functional inequality. Synthetic experiments demonstrate FI convergence and the benefit of each mechanism. Bayesian fine-tuning experiments with LLMs and vision-language models support our oracle model and show that RA-LMC matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

title: Guide pour une intégration réussie de l’IA au sein des organisations
abstract: Plusieurs organisations (publiques, privées et à but non lucratif) ont intégré des outils d’IA dans leurs activités ou sont en train de se familiariser avec ceux-ci. Cependant, de nombreuses études montrent que, malgré des attentes élevées et des investissements importants, la plupart d’entre elles n’ont pas encore constaté de gains mesurables en matière de productivité, de chiffre d’affaires ou de retour sur investissement. Le retour sur investissement peut tarder à se concrétiser, puisque les grandes innovations technologiques mettent souvent plus de dix ans à produire des retombées économiques mesurables. L’objectif de ce guide est de fournir aux organisations des stratégies pour intégrer avec succès les outils d’IA et de proposer de bonnes pratiques permettant d’utiliser ces outils de manière efficace et responsable. La version préliminaire du guide s’appuie sur une revue des lignes directrices, des cadres et des guides sur l’intégration de l’IA publiés par des organisations publiques, privées et à but non lucratif au Canada et à l’international, ainsi que sur des études scientifiques récentes. Le guide a ensuite été bonifié à partir des résultats de l'étude, qui repose sur des données recueillies auprès de gestionnaires, de développeurs et de formateurs de quatre secteurs au Québec : l’économie sociale et l’action communautaire, la finance, les ressources humaines et les technologies de l’information.

abstract: This research reviews published studies on how long-context and multi-turn interaction affect agentic language models. title: Convergence Between Artificial Intelligence and Digital Purchasing Behavior
authors: Célia Maria Ramos Serra Reis Barroso
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming digital behavior and consumer decision-making, reshaping interactions between individuals and brands across digital platforms. This chapter analyzes the relationship between digital behavior, AI, and marketing strategies in a changing technological context. It examines how AI-driven tools, such as predictive analytics and automated recommendation systems, enable content personalization, improve user experiences, and increase marketing effectiveness. Based on contemporary literature and secondary data from sources including Statista, Pew Research Center, Pordata and Euromonitor, the study adopts an exploratory approach to assess AI's impact on consumer engagement and strategic marketing practices. It also discusses ethical challenges, such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and manipulation risks. The research offers insights for scholars and practitioners on AI's growing influence and highlights the need for future qualitative studies on consumer perceptions.

title: A Hybrid deep learning model for effective segmentation and classification of lung nodules from CT images
abstract: Deep learning algorithms will be used to detect lung nodule anomalies at an earlier stage. The primary goal of this effort is to properly identify lung cancer, which is critical in preserving a person’s life. Lung cancer has been a source of concern for people all around the world for decades. Several researchers presented numerous issues and solutions for various stages of a computer-aided system for diagnosing lung cancer in its early stages, as well as information about lung cancer. Computer vision is one of the field of artificial intelligence this is a better way to detect and prevent the lung cancer. This study focuses on the stages involved in detecting lung tumor regions, namely pre-processing, segmentation, and classification models. An adaptive median filter is used in pre-processing to identify the noise. The work’s originality seeks to create a simple yet effective model for the rapid identification and U-net architecture based segmentation of lung nodules. This approach focuses on the identification and segmentation of lung cancer by detecting picture normalcy and abnormalities.

title: Role-Guided Risk-Aware Attention for Multi-AUV Target-Zone Reaching under Active Defense
abstract: Cooperative target-zone reaching by multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) under active defense remains challenging because each vehicle must make sequential guidance decisions under nonlinear hydrodynamics, sonar-limited perception, obstacle constraints, and defender interference. This paper proposes a role-guided risk-aware attention variant of multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), termed role-guided risk-aware attention MADDPG (RGRA-MADDPG), for attacker-side multi-AUV target-zone reaching under active defense. Different from homogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies, the proposed method assigns mission-specific roles to the AUVs, including a Primary Attack AUV, a Coordinated Strike AUV, and a Bait AUV. A role-conditioned attention module is developed to help each AUV selectively emphasize targets, defenders, obstacles, and teammates from local observations, while a risk-prior bias introduces interpretable obstacle-, defender-, and target-related cues into the attention scores. The framework is trained under centralized training and executed through decentralized local policies. Comparative simulations, perturbation tests, mechanism-isolation studies, and physical-response validation are used to evaluate target-reaching success, cooperative behavior, robustness, and command feasibility. Results show that the proposed method improves adversarial target-zone reaching performance over standard MADDPG-based variants while producing differentiated and interpretable multi-AUV tactics.

title: Real-Time Traffic Density Estimation: A Hybrid Computer Vision and Predictive Machine Learning Pipeline
abstract: Traffic density estimation from camera feeds requires connecting visual perception with short-horizon forecasting. We present a two-stage pipeline that combines vehicle detection and tracking with a spatial logic layer, followed by a temporal estimator. The spatial layer filters bounding boxes by their overlap with a precomputed road mask and extracts per-frame traffic features. LSTM, GRU, and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) estimators use these features to predict five future steps from a ten-frame input window. We benchmark ten detector variants from six families on a dataset of 5,716 annotated frames using a single NVIDIA GPU. YOLOv5l achieves the highest mAP@50:95 of 0.524 at 56 frames per second, while YOLOv8n reaches 258 frames per second at 0.487 mAP@50:95; these rates measure detector inference without tracking or spatial filtering. Temporal evaluation on 29,243 held-out windows yields aggregate R-squared values of 0.858 for GRU, 0.856 for LSTM, and 0.840 for TCN. These metrics measure forecasts of detector-derived telemetry and are dominated by direction variance, rather than establishing absolute traffic-density accuracy. No road mask was available for the evaluation stream, limiting validation of the spatial filtering component. A live run on a third camera stream examines forecasting behavior within the complete pipeline. The results characterize detector speed-accuracy trade-offs and the limitations of short-window traffic telemetry forecasting.

title: SBNO : Schrödinger Bridge Neural Operator for the Forward and Inverse Problems under Missing Information
abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schrödinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.

title: A robust digital receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

title: Volume Rendering with Metric--Phase Fields for Thin Structures and Sign-Ambiguous Geometry
abstract: Neural implicit surface methods that couple volume rendering with signed distance functions (SDFs), such as VolSDF and NeuS, achieve high-quality multi-view reconstruction for watertight objects. However, these approaches rely on a globally consistent inside-outside partition of space. This assumption becomes fragile for thin structures (e.g., sheets, tubes, and thin walls) and can break down for sign-ambiguous geometry (e.g., surfaces with boundary, non-manifold junctions, and closely spaced surface components), often resulting in spurious closures or loss of fine structures. Unsigned distance field (UDF) formulations relax the global sign requirement and better support non-watertight geometry, but are substantially harder to optimize. We propose PhaseSurf, a neural volume rendering framework built on Metric-Phase Fields (MPFs). MPFs decompose geometry into a nonnegative metric field capturing unsigned proximity and a continuous phase field providing a soft sign cue. By coupling the two through residual phase injection, MPFs yield a signed composite implicit function with stable near-surface gradients while retaining UDF-like robustness in sign-ambiguous regions. This design enables direct iso-surface extraction using standard Marching Cubes and avoids the failure modes of both pure SDF- and UDF-based formulations. We further introduce MPF-specific training losses that enforce metric consistency, stabilize phase transitions near the interface, and suppress spurious geometry in free space. Experiments on multi-view datasets with thin structures and sign-ambiguous geometry show that PhaseSurf produces more stable reconstructions and higher-quality geometry than UDF-based methods and recent 3DGS pipelines, while avoiding artifacts typical of SDF-based approaches.

title: EXPERIMENTAL COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF NAIVE BAYES AND RULE BASED DECISION TREE PERFORMANCE IN ATTRIBUTIVE CLASSIFICATION OF SCHOLARLY ARTICLES
abstract: Document classification categorizes documents based on their attributes or contents to determine how they will be stored, retrieved, and shared. Improper classification of documents can lead to significant waste of time, resources, productivity, and efficiency in organizational information management systems. This study presents the Experimental Comparative Analysis (ECA) of Naive Bayes Model (NBM) and Rule-Based Decision Tree Model (RBDTM) in the classification of journal articles based on their attributes such as Name of Journal (NOJ) regarded as the specific domain, Peer Reviewed (PR) status, Volume Information (VI), the Title (T), Author Names (AN), Digital Object Identifier (DOI) and Keywords (KW). The models were trained based on direct algebraic solutions, saved parameters, and deterministic passes without gradient descent updates, using supervised Machine Learning (ML) approach and K-fold validation sampling technique for training and testing. Performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, program execution time, information retrieval response time, memory usage, and confusion matrix were used for analysis and evaluation. The training and testing datasets were obtained from open-licensed, peer-reviewed journal articles from Africa, Asia, the United States of America, Eastern and Western Europe. The average test results at the baseline threshold showed that the NBM performed better than the RBDTM in accuracy, recall, and F1-score (68%, 68%, and 80.6%, respectively); both models achieved 100% precision and 0% specificity. In contrast, RBDTM outperformed NBM in program execution time, information retrieval response time, and memory usage (17.19ms, 7.44ms, and 0.13%, respectively). At the optimized threshold, both models tied with 100% accuracy, 100% precision, 100% recall, 0% specificity, and 100% F1-score, but the RBDTM demonstrated the best overall performance with 18.2ms program execution time, 7.74ms information retrieval response time, and 0.14% memory usage.

title: Code and data for "Physically constrained adversarial attacks on neural-network classifiers of quantum phases: symmetry-breaking versus topological order"
abstract: Simulation code, generated datasets, trained network weights, raw results files and figure scripts accompanying the manuscript “Physically constrained adversarial attacks on neural-network classifiers of quantum phases: symmetry-breaking versus topological order”, submitted to Quantum Frontiers. Contents: Monte Carlo generation of two-dimensional Ising configurations (L = 16); generation of Su–Schrieffer–Heeger chains (N = 96) with chiral-symmetric hopping disorder and real-space winding number; MLP, periodic CNN and Z2-symmetrised CNN classifiers; FGSM/PGD, greedy spin-flip and Hamiltonian-level hopping-disorder attacks; adversarial training; and all results from which the figures and tables in the paper are produced. See README.md for the file list and reproduction steps. Tested with Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, PyTorch 2.14 (CPU) and Matplotlib 3.11.

title: QuantumShield AI: An AI-Powered Post-Quantum Cryptography Recommendation Platform
abstract: The finalization of the NIST post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), with FN-DSA (draft FIPS 206), has shifted the migration question from whether to adopt PQC to which standard best fits an organization's operational and regulatory context. Existing studies benchmark these algorithms thoroughly but stop short of a selection mechanism, leaving practitioners to interpret timing tables by hand. This paper presents QuantumShield AI, a decision-support platform that formalizes PQC algorithm selection as a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) problem, encodes the selection task as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), and solves it with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on a statevector simulator, cross-validated by an exact classical solver. Six industry profiles — banking, healthcare, IoT/edge, government, e-commerce, and defense supply criteria weightings grounded in sector requirements. The framework is delivered as a three-tier platform combining a React front end, a Spring Boot service layer with JWT-based role-controlled access, and a Python/Qiskit quantum microservice over PostgreSQL. To our knowledge this is the first framework to operationalize selection across the complete finalized NIST portfolio, converting sector requirements into an auditable, reproducible recommendation. Across all six profiles the QAOA solution recovers the exact optimum (approximation ratio = 1.0), validating the pipeline; we are explicit that at the four-algorithm scale this certifies correctness rather than quantum advantage, and the QUBO–QAOA formulation is carried as a forward-compatible path to NP-hard enterprise-portfolio selection. The contribution is a novel, deployable decision methodology and its engineered realization.

title: Field Notes from a Low-Cost Robot Learning Lab: Hardware Churn, Software Whiplash, and What Actually Went Wrong
abstract: This is the informal companion to two more rigorous papers from the same project. Over roughly seven weeks we trained imitation-learning policies on a self-built SO-101 robot arm, and along the way we moved the work between machines more often than planned, rebuilt the camera setup, fought a fast-moving open-source framework, and lost an embarrassing amount of time to causes that turned out to be a loose power cable, a swapped port, or a missing audio package. The quantified findings are reported elsewhere. Here we tell the rest: what the hardware and software path actually looked like, which incidents cost us the most time and why, what we would warn a newcomer about, and which threads we deliberately left unfinished. We write for people building something similar on a hobbyist budget, not for reviewers, and we try to be as candid about our mistakes as about our results.

title: Identifiability Under Runtime Shielding
abstract: This methods note examines what can be inferred about an agent when a runtime safety shield mediates its proposed actions. Different proposals can produce identical safe executions, so agreement in executed behaviour does not necessarily imply agreement in proposal distributions. Conversely, distinguishable proposal distributions do not by themselves identify a unique internal mechanism or establish its causal contribution. Three elementary propositions address conditional safety invariance, observational collapse under shielding, and restricted injectivity on a declared family of proposal distributions. Worked examples explain why an intervention witness may remain insufficient, why full channel rank does not guarantee useful finite-sample discrimination, and why observations that are individually innocuous may jointly disclose sensitive information. PDE-DI is presented as a measurement procedure for documenting the target contrast, permitted probes and observations, execution semantics, channel calibration, disclosure constraints, uncertainty, and interpretation limits. It distinguishes executed violations, disallowed proposals, and mediator interventions. Unidentifiability or inadequate measurement precision must not be interpreted as equivalence or a negative causal finding. Causal attribution requires a separate design with justified interventions, appropriate comparisons, and an explicit causal estimand. The reported technical evidence is a finite reference program that enumerates 2,187 trajectories and 13,122 transitions and checks seven mathematical assertion groups. These are reference checks, not independent empirical trials. The program contains no developmental learning, autonomous agent, or Purple implementation. The literature discussion is a targeted comparison with 30 references and explicitly stated source-access limitations. Appendix A outlines the Purple developmental research programme as a possible future application, including untested hypotheses and requirements for a valid component-effect study. The supported contribution is an explicit, worked measurement framework based on established arguments. No new general theorem, empirical superiority, distinctive Purple functionality, or mechanistic novelty is established. This record contains the English and Hungarian manuscripts, version 0.3, dated 9 October 2026. The manuscripts disclose generative AI assistance in drafting, translation, and consistency checking.

abstract: The geopolitical issue between Israel and Palestine has sparked a wide range of public reactions on social media, particularly on the platform X. Sentiment analysis is a widely discussed topic in Natural Language Processing.This study develops a sentiment classification model for that issue using the BERT Base Uncased architecture, with data labeled automatically through the VADER approach.Data were collected via scraping with Tweet-Harvest, yielding 3,172 tweets, later reduced to 2,362 after preprocessing stages including cleaning, case folding, tokenizing, stopword removal, and stemming.VADER labeling produced a distribution of 73.7% negative sentiment and 26.3% positive sentiment.The model achieved 87.34% accuracy, with precision, recall, and F1-Score for the negative class of 92%, 90%, and 91%, respectively, while the positive class obtained 74%, 79%, and 77%.The macro-average F1-score reached 84%, reflecting the model's performance across both classes with equal weighting despite the imbalanced data distribution.These results indicate that BERT Base Uncased can classify VADER-generated labels with fairly good performance in the context of international geopolitical issues.Kata

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Electric Vehicle Charging in a Time-varying Hierarchical Infrastructure
abstract: Uncertainty quantification for electric vehicle (EV) charging demand is essential to turn the increasing pressure of EV adoption on power systems into a source of flexibility. We study a large-scale dataset of public charging stations in Scotland, where demand exhibits a hierarchical structure, organized across multiple aggregation levels, from individual charging points to regional and national scales. The charging infrastructure is continuously evolving, with new stations deployed and existing ones occasionally removed, which calls for forecasting and uncertainty quantification methods tailored to this evolving structure. To address these challenges, we combine hierarchical forecasting with recent advances in conformal prediction with missing data. The conformal procedures considered produce valid prediction intervals at every node of the hierarchy and the algorithm CP-MNR-Nested successfully accounts for the time-varying hierarchical structure of the data.

title: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.

title: Quantum Information-Theoretic Analysis of Optical Fiber Sensing via Stimulated Brillouin Scattering
abstract: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) is a powerful mechanism for distributed sensing in optical fibers, as the Brillouin response is highly sensitive to local material parameters. Assuming the input probe is a quantum state, we develop a quantum-information-theoretic framework for SBS-based fiber sensing and intrusion detection. Starting from a linearized opto-acoustic Hamiltonian, we derive an effective input-output relation for a short fiber segment. We then model each fiber segment as a single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel and the entire fiber as a cascade of quantum channels. We then compute the quantum Fisher information for general SBS-dependent parameters and identify optimal measurement settings to achieve the quantum limit, comparing them with receiver-constrained strategies such as heterodyne detection and photon counting. In addition, we propose an adaptive approach that achieves first-order asymptotic optimality and provides a novel second-order correction to address preliminary miscalibration. As an application, we apply the framework to the fiber-tapping detection problem.

title: Unreliable Narrator Framing as a Cost-effective Mechanism for Satire Explanation of Australian and American Satirical News
abstract: Satirical news is a unique form of misinformation: it is intended to be humorous by the original publication source but can be misinterpreted. Explanation of satirical news articles is challenging because recent and local context needs to be incorporated. This is a pilot study that explores explanation generation for satirical news articles from Australia and compares them alongside those from USA. The paper demonstrates that framing explanations on unreliable narrator theory on open-weights models can be a feasible, cost-effective alternative to frontier models. We find that models identify the satirical tropes more accurately on the American source than the Australian one. This work results in a novel dataset and an evaluation benchmark for satirical explanation.

title: A Simple Explicit Construction of Smaller Strong Blocking Sets
abstract: Alon, Bishnoi, Das and Neri constructed sequences of strong blocking sets in $(k-1)$-dimension projective space $P({\bf F}_q, k-1)$ with sizes at most $Cqk$, where $k$ goes to the infinity and $C$ is a fixed positive constant not depending on $q$, in their paper published in Transactions AMS, vol. 277, pp. 5389-5410, 2024. This is equivalent to a sequence of minimal $[n_i,k_i]_q$ codes with positive rate $\frac{k_i}{n_i} \geq c$, where $k_i$ goes to the infinity and $c$ is a fixed positive constant only depending on $q$. They solved one of the main open problems on minimal codes. The Alon-Bishnoi-Das-Neri construction was based on asymptotically good sequences of algebraic geometric codes and expander graphs. However, the constant $C$ is large for small prime power $q$. In this paper, based on a simple approach using $(q-1)$-power intersecting algebraic geometric codes via concatenation to construct minimal codes, we construct explicit strong blocking sets in $(k-1)$-dimension projective space with sizes around $2(q^2-1)k$, equivalently, explicit minimal $[n,k]_q$ codes with length around $2(q^2-1)k$. This is an essential improvement on the previous result of Alon-Bishnoi-Das-Neri, when $q \leq 11$. For large $q$, strong blocking sets and minimal codes in our construction are worse than the previous construction of Alon-Bishnoi-Das-Neri. However, our approach is much simpler and does not depend on expander graphs.
